oa:W7124821740.title: Simulazione, natura umana e ricerca della verità nel pensiero di Agostino, Tommaso d’Aquino e Bonaventura da Bagnoregio
oa:W7124821740.abstract: In this article we analyze the reflection pursued by Augustine, Thomas Aquinas, and Bonaventure on the relation between simulation, human nature, and search for the truth. In his commentary on the “fall” of the Progenitors, contained in De Genesi contra Manichaeos, Augustine sees in the simulation of the condition of nudity as the reason for hiding from God not only a simple going away from truth, but a far more dangerous detachment from the simplicity and, at the same time, from the high dignity of the human being. In the great medieval Scholasticism, both Thomas and Bonaventure resume Augustine’s reflection, adapting and systematizing it within their own reflection on the human being and on the Church. Thomas Aquinas puts in relation simulation with hypocrisy, underlining how the fact of pretending to be someone else leads to the wilting of the awareness of being God’s creature; in this sense, the sinner who simulates integrity loses himself and becomes unaware of himself. In the Collationes in Hexaemeron, Bonaventure compares the abandonment of simplicity and the going away from the source of truth by the Progenitors to the Church going away from its original simplicity: just like Adam and Eve preferred simulation to truth and knowledge to beatitude in Eden, so the Church abandoned its original simplicity by assuming a posture of false zeal for the Law, driven by a sterile science that tends towards the search for God.

oa:W7125627637.title: THE LAZY GOD DOES NOT PLAY SUDOKU Quantum Indeterminacy, Ontological Laziness, and Why the World Was Already Solved Before You Looked (A polemical essay in dialogue with Slavoj Žižek)
oa:W7125627637.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7125627637.abstract: Slavoj Žižek has famously suggested that quantum mechanics reveals a fundamentally unfinished reality: a world that hesitates, fails to fully actualize itself, and only becomes determinate through acts of observation. This idea is often framed through the metaphor of a “lazy God” who economizes on ontology, much like a video game that renders the world only when the player approaches it. In this essay, I argue that this metaphor is deeply misleading. By replacing the video game with a different and less glamorous model—the Sudoku puzzle—I propose an alternative ontological reading of quantum indeterminacy. On this view, indeterminacy is not ontological but epistemic, not a feature of reality itself but of our perspectival access to a globally fixed structure. The essay connects this claim to a higher-dimensional ontological framework and to a model of post-realization modal collapse, according to which the world is fully determined once it occurs, even if it remains locally opaque. The result is a direct challenge to the “lazy God” thesis and a defense of a radically non-creative, non-dynamic ontology.

oa:W7125692143.title: Analysis of Existential (Wujūdī) and Intuitive (Shuhūdī) Approaches in Islamic Mysticism
oa:W7125692143.venue: Integrated Journal for Research in Arts and Humanities
oa:W7125692143.abstract: Waḥdat al-Wujūd (Unity of Being) in mystical literature is akin to a subtle seasoning whose flavor varies with each temperament; through it, Ṣūfī poetry has ascended to the loftiest planes of truth and metaphor. Owing to the doctrine of Unity of Being, Islamic literature was enriched as a distinct style and intellectual school. Poetry acquired a genuine ardor, the savor of sincerity, and the delicacy and hues of fervent love; mystical literature spread across the world, and hundreds of works were composed within this tradition, forming vast libraries in their own right. On the other hand, the theory of Waḥdat al-Shuhūd (Unity of Witnessing) presents a content ostensibly opposed to that of Waḥdat al-Wujūd; yet Hamza Baba and several other mystics regard this opposition as merely a verbal dispute. Many Ṣūfīs have described the ultimate stage of witnessing with the expression “all is from Him”, by which they mean that the presence of the One God is perceived in the existence of everything, and that the cosmos is but the shadow (ẓill) of the Divine attributes, not the attributes themselves for the attribute is never identical with the Essence. The notion of shadow signifies that the existence of a thing manifests itself in second, third, fourth levels, and so on. Here, the controversy surrounding Waḥdat al-Wujūd becomes exceedingly subtle and complex; it is therefore necessary that the general public not be drawn into this debate, for the discourse exceeds the bounds of common understanding. oa:W7125766369.title: Multiplicity Without Distinction? Divine Ideas and Simplicity in Thomas Aquinas
oa:W7125766369.abstract: This paper examines whether Thomas Aquinas’s doctrine of divine exemplarism can be coherently reconciled with his commitment to divine simplicity. In Thomas’s view, God creates by means of certaindivine ideas called exemplars, which serve as the formal causes of creatures, and are located in the divine mind. These exemplar ideas are many, since each individual creature has a respective exemplar from which it receives its form. However, Thomas is simultaneously committed to a rigid form of divine simplicity, according to which the divine ideas are ontologically identical to the divine essence. This gives rise to the main question of this paper: Can a multiplicity of divine ideas, each serving as a distinct exemplar for a particular creature, be compatible with a God who is metaphysically simple and devoid of internal distinctions? After explicating Thomas’ views on the divine ideas as well as divine simplicity, the paper argues that the divine ideas need real ontological relations to their respective objects in the world in order to function as extrinsic formal causes, which Thomas views them as. It further argues that any ontological relation to one divine idea necessitates it being a relation to the divine essence as a whole, since all divine ideas are ontologically identical to God’s essence. Given Thomas’ belief that any creature is perfectly like its respective exemplar in form, and that the exemplar is identical to the divine essence, it seems to follow that any creature should be identical in form to the divine essence. Such a result threatens to collapse the distinction between God and creation, risking pantheistic implications incompatible with Thomas’ metaphysics.

oa:W7127111392.title: Modal Collapse and the Migdal Effect: A Coherence-Based Detector Framework
oa:W7127111392.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7127111392.abstract: The Migdal effect—electron excitation or ionization induced by sudden nuclear recoil—has emerged as a critical detection channel in low-threshold dark matter experiments. This work reinterprets the Migdal effect within the framework of Unified Vibrational Field Theory (UVFT), treating it not as anomalous sub-threshold energy transfer but as a localized coherence failure. We propose a physically grounded, detector-internal realization of quantum collapse and identify Migdal processes as the first experimental anchor for UVFT. Collapse is shown to result from coherence strain exceeding a survival threshold, requiring no observer or external measurement axiom. This includes original coherence-gradient criteria, survival threshold derivations, and detector response models for modal ejection—all constructed within UVFT’s geometric coherence framework.

oa:W7127372555.title: The Mystery of Awe and Silence at the Level of the Uniqueness of Divine Essence: The Views of Avicenna, Mullā Ṣadrā, and ʿAllāma Ṭabāṭaāʾī
oa:W7127372555.venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
oa:W7127372555.abstract: Abstract In their theological works, Muslim philosophers tend to elaborate on the unity and other attributes of the Necessary Existent (wājib al-wujūd) after establishing its existence. In such discussions, they examine the essence (dhāt) alongside its attributes but remain silent regarding the essence independent of the attributes. In some of their works, Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), Mullā Ṣadrā, and ʿAllāma Ṭabāṭabāʾī address the reasoning behind this silence. Drawing upon the principle of simplicity (bisāṭa) and the transcendence (tanazzuh) of the essence from any form of composition or multiplicity, Avicenna arrives at the theory of the conceptual unity of attributes. He considers essential attributes such as knowledge and power to be inextricable concomitants (lawāzim) of, and posterior to, the essence. From Ṣadr al-Mutaʾallihīn’s perspective, all determinations dissolve in the Unique Essence (al-dhāt al-aḥadiyya), while attributes, names, and their manifestations are collectively present at the level of Oneness (wāḥidiyya). ʿAllāma Ṭabāṭabāʾī holds that each of God's perfectional attributes (al-ṣifāt al-kamāliyya) encompasses other perfections. Emphasizing the absoluteness of the essence and distinguishing between the two ranks of Uniqueness (aḥadiyya) and Oneness (wāḥidiyya), Ṭabāṭabāʾī regards names and attributes as posterior to the rank of essence. Given the indescribability of the essence, any discourse on the Unique Essence is deemed impossible. The present study employs a descriptive-analytical method, seeking to examine the philosophical silence in confronting the Unique Essence by analyzing the views of Ibn Sīnā, Mullā Ṣadrā, and ʿAllāma Ṭabāṭabāʾī. Keywords Simplicity, absoluteness, uniqueness (aḥadiyya), silence, Ibn Sīnā (Avicenna), Mullā Ṣadrā, ʿAllāma Ṭabāṭa

oa:W7128002911.title: Consciousness as the Phenomenological Experience of Finitude: Temporal Asymmetry and the Global Determination of the World
oa:W7128002911.abstract: This paper develops a conception of consciousness compatible with a model of global ontological determination and a block universe ontology of time. It argues that consciousness should not be understood as an additional faculty, substance, or ontological opening, but rather as the phenomenological experience proper to a finite being embedded in a world that is ontologically complete and temporally non-dynamic. In such a framework, time does not “flow” or “pass”; instead, past, present, and future coexist within the structure of the world in the same sense as spatial dimensions. What appears to “flow” is the phenomenological experience of a finite agent whose epistemic access to the world is temporally asymmetric. The paper integrates a post-realization modal collapse framework, according to which genuine ontological possibility exists only prior to the realization of a single world. Once realization occurs, the modal space collapses and the world becomes globally determined. Within this ontological setting, the experience of temporal passage, deliberation, and openness is shown to arise not from any ontological becoming, but from the asymmetric epistemic access of finite agents to a temporally extended but ontologically static world. Consciousness is thus reconceived as the necessary phenomenological correlate of finitude in a block universe, rather than as an anomaly requiring metaphysical supplementation.

oa:W7128120665.title: Existence Without Essence: An Invariance-Structural Approach to Modality
oa:W7128120665.abstract: This paper develops Invariance-Structural Ontology (Sigma_IS), a formal axiomatic system in first-order modal logic that grounds object identity in the preservation of structural invariants across admissible modal transformations, rather than in static substance. Working within S4 constant-domain semantics, the paper provides: (1) A core set of axioms avoiding second-order quantification; (2) An explicit finite Kripke countermodel that rigorously refutes modal collapse; and (3) A detailed Henkin-style canonical construction establishing the system's consistency and completeness. The result is a logically robust framework that reconciles existential necessity with qualitative contingency, offering a "Dynamic Parmenidean" alternative to both radical structuralism and strong necessitarianism.

oa:W7128127253.title: Positive Modal Ontology: The Resolution of Dynamic Plenitude V2
oa:W7128127253.abstract: ​This paper presents the formal axioms of a Positive Modal Ontology (\Sigma_{PMO}) formulated within first-order modal logic S4 under constant-domain semantics. A finite countermodel is constructed to demonstrate the failure of the modal collapse schema (MC): \phi \rightarrow \Box \phi, utilizing the distinction between Latency (P) and Actuality (A). A Henkin-style canonical model construction is provided in the appendix to establish the semantic legitimacy and internal consistency of the system, offering a rigorous solution to the problem of movement within a necessitist framework.

oa:W7128142264.title: From Grounding to the Aseity Fork: Why Nominalism and Divine Conceptualism Fall Short
oa:W7128142264.abstract: Recent philosophy of religion increasingly casts divine ultimacy in the idiom of grounding: God would be fundamental (ungrounded) and everything else dependent on God. The Aseity Fork result sharpens that picture: a creator with full aseity—independent from causes and any other conditions—cannot be both distinct and ultimate. Either God is identical with Existence itself (the Identity horn of the Aseity Fork), or any distinct theistic agent operates within Existence through non-identical enabling structures (the Personal Inside horn), thereby compromising full robust aseity. This paper closes the remaining standard escape routes to the Fork invoked in the grounding/abstracta literature: (1) nominalism (“no abstracta, so no prior framework”), (2) divine conceptualism (“abstracta are divine thoughts”), (3) simplicity-identification (“God is the Law of Non-Contradiction / the order”), and (4) the linguistic retreat (“logic binds talk, not God”). The central clarification is that the relevant “structure” is not a Platonic inventory but a constraint-profile: the minimal reality-side conditions for determinacy, contentful cognition, and contrast-fixing (“this rather than that”). The argument is neutral on Platonism vs nominalism, truthmaker maximalism, thick theories of truth, and classical vs non-classical consequence; it assumes only minimal truth-aptness (a determinate correct/incorrect contrast). Once the target is fixed at the constraint level, nominalism and conceptualism either (i) collapse into Identity (if God is identified with the whole-level contrast-fixing order), or (ii) concede Personal Inside dependence for being/acting (if that order is non-identical). oa:W7128142627.title: A Positive Modal Ontology: A First-Order Formal Alternative to Kantian Limitation
oa:W7128142627.abstract: Article Summary The article develops a formal system in First-Order Modal Logic (S4) that articulates a positive monist ontology. Its central claims are: Being is necessary — something exists in every possible world. Non-Being is not an ontological entity, but merely the absence of modal actualization. Potency is distinct from Act — not everything that can happen must happen. Acts are contingent, which blocks modal collapse (unlike S5). No act occurs ex nihilo — every actualization depends on Being. Reality is, in principle, cognizable — there is no ontological “outside” beyond intelligibility. The Kantian noumenal barrier is rejected: there is no unknowable thing-in-itself separate from the modal–rational structure of reality. Result: The article does not prove the truth of the ontology, but it does prove its formal coherence. It shows that a non-skeptical, post-Kantian metaphysics can be logically consistent, non-trivial, and formally defensible, without collapsing into determinism or pre-critical dogmatism.

oa:W7128568670.title: Theism vs. Naturalism: A Cumulative Bayesian Assessment of Explanatory Power
oa:W7128568670.abstract: This paper presents a cumulative Bayesian analysis comparing the explanatory power of Theism (T) and Naturalism (N). Drawing upon the methodological frameworks of Swinburne and Oppy, the study evaluates a comprehensive set of arguments, including cosmological and teleological arguments, the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, and arguments concerning logical coherence. By assigning epistemic probability ranges to each evidential factor, the posterior probabilities of the competing hypotheses are calculated under lower-bound, upperbound, and average scenarios. The results indicate that while Theism receives significant support from fine-tuning and consciousness, the cumulative weight of existential and logical defeaters—specifically the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, and modal collapse—renders Naturalism the dominant hypothesis with a probability exceeding 89% in the realistic average scenario.

oa:W7130363180.title: Another Failed Modal Collapse Argument
oa:W7130363180.abstract: Abstract The doctrine of divine simplicity says that God is not composed of parts (physical or metaphysical). Modal collapse arguments aim to show that the necessary co-existence of God and creation follows from the doctrine. As noted by Christopher Tomaszewski, R. T. Mullins’s version of this argument assumes that a crucial term occurring within its premises is rigid, leaving the argument invalid or question begging. I examine a recent attempt by Mullins to repair his argument and defend the rigidity of this term. Mullins assumes a test for discerning rigidity on which he and Tomaszewski agree. I argue that this test is false and then provide a new test. My test bodes ill for modal collapse arguments in general.

oa:W7130515722.title: Did Irenaeus Influence Novatian’s View of Divine Simplicity?
oa:W7130515722.abstract: This article traces the influence of Irenaeus into the third century by arguing that Novatian’s argument regarding the unity of divine will, thought, and action (Novatian, De Trinitate 5-6) draws from Irenaeus (Contra Haereses 2.13 and 1.12). For Novatian, God’s works immediately follow his will, for God is all eye, all ear, and simple (Novatian, De Trinitate 6.7). This same structure is found in Irenaeus, who argues that God is simple and that God, “as soon as He thinks, also performs what He has willed,” for God is “all mind, and all thought, etc.” (Contra Haereses 1.12.2; 2.13). This article notes where, in this passage, Novatian uses the same concepts, terms, and sequence. If this view of Novatian’s dependence is correct, it would demonstrate the influence of Irenaeus on the fourth of Lewis Ayre’s four theological trajectories that influenced Nicaea.

oa:W7130946670.title: Beyond Proof: Divine Simplicity, Structural Axiology, and the Limits of Logic
oa:W7130946670.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7130946670.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper critiques the "proof paradigm," a contemporary argument that uses Gödel-Tarski limitative theorems to suggest a class of truths remains 'necessarily unprovable' even for an omniscient God, positing a metaphysical divide between truth and provability. We contend this argument is susceptible to a fundamental category error: it projects 'proof'—understood as a finite, discursive, and system-relative creaturely epistemic tool—univocally onto the divine intellect. In response, we propose a constructive theological epistemology through a synthesis of two frameworks. Divine Simplicity, the classical doctrine that God's knowledge is a simple, eternal, and causative act identical with His essence, challenges the applicability of discursive 'proof' to divine cognition. Structural Axiology, formalized via Category Theory, models the content of this simple knowledge as involving a sovereign choice among incommensurable value categories (C_W1: Redemptive Struggle, C_W2: Perfect Harmony, C_W3: Immanent Secular Virtue). Our synthesis thereby recontextualizes the limitative results: Gödelian incompleteness is interpreted as describing a structural feature intrinsic to certain created logical orders (notably C_W3), rather than necessarily representing a constraint on divine cognition itself. This contributes to the development of a post-proof theological epistemology, which seeks to recalibrate pivotal debates by offering an alternative to Leibnizian optimization models of divine freedom, proposing a theistic interpretative framework for mathematics, and reframing the problem of evil within the paradigm of Redemptive Struggle.

oa:W7130963917.title: Beyond Proof: Divine Simplicity, Structural Axiology, and the Limits of Logic
oa:W7130963917.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7130963917.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper critiques the "proof paradigm," a contemporary argument that uses Gödel-Tarski limitative theorems to suggest a class of truths remains 'necessarily unprovable' even for an omniscient God, positing a metaphysical divide between truth and provability. We contend this argument is susceptible to a fundamental category error: it projects 'proof'—understood as a finite, discursive, and system-relative creaturely epistemic tool—univocally onto the divine intellect. In response, we propose a constructive theological epistemology through a synthesis of two frameworks. Divine Simplicity, the classical doctrine that God's knowledge is a simple, eternal, and causative act identical with His essence, challenges the applicability of discursive 'proof' to divine cognition. Structural Axiology, formalized via Category Theory, models the content of this simple knowledge as involving a sovereign choice among incommensurable value categories (C_W1: Redemptive Struggle, C_W2: Perfect Harmony, C_W3: Immanent Secular Virtue). Our synthesis thereby recontextualizes the limitative results: Gödelian incompleteness is interpreted as describing a structural feature intrinsic to certain created logical orders (notably C_W3), rather than necessarily representing a constraint on divine cognition itself. This contributes to the development of a post-proof theological epistemology, which seeks to recalibrate pivotal debates by offering an alternative to Leibnizian optimization models of divine freedom, proposing a theistic interpretative framework for mathematics, and reframing the problem of evil within the paradigm of Redemptive Struggle.

oa:W7131776975.title: Gödel’s Ontological Proof of the Existence of God and its Consistency Consequences
oa:W7131776975.abstract: Gödel’s ontological proof of God’s existence, finalized in 1970, constitutes one of the most ambitious attempts to formalize metaphysical theology using modern logic. Rooted in a tradition stretching from Anselm through Descartes and Leibniz, Gödel’s argument reformulates the classical ontological proof in higher-order modal logic. Yet its significance extends far beyond theology. When stripped of modalities, Gödel’s axioms define an ultrafilter, thereby connecting metaphysical reasoning with foundational set theory and strong axioms of infinity. This talk reconstructs the historical development of ontological arguments, analyzes Gödel’s formal system, examines the phenomenon of modal collapse, and explores the unexpected implications for mathematical foundations, showing that consistency of arithmetic and ZFC is a consequence of the ontological proof. It is argued that Gödel’s proof should be understood not primarily as a theological demonstration but as a profound structural experiment revealing deep connections between logic, metaphysics, and infinity.

oa:W7131791004.title: Contemplating Divine Simplicity
oa:W7131791004.abstract: Is divine simplicity coherent? Is there adequate theological and philosophical motivation for the doctrine? Does it undermine God’s freedom in creation? Does it help or hinder Trinitarian doctrine? For the first time in a multi-view format, a team of renowned proponents and critics of divine simplicity come together to consider these questions and discuss the intrinsic merits of the doctrine.With contributors presenting Thomistic, Anselmian, Eastern Orthodox and Scotistic views, as well as a sustained and considered critique, this unique structure makes for a genuine discussion and developed exploration of the key issues at stake. Chapters evaluate the coherence and interpretation of divine simplicity, assessing which version is worthy of assent, and set out the motivations in favour of the doctrine. Divine freedom, the contingency of creation and the doctrine of the Trinity are also considered in light of theological arguments against divine simplicity. A valuable resource for any scholar or student of philosophy of religion and theology,Contemplating Divine Simplicitybrings into dialogue diverse views of five thinkers, tracing the arguments in favour of divine simplicity from divine aseity.

oa:W7131911353.title: 'Jonathan Edwards's God: The Trinity, Individuation and Divine Simplicity'
oa:W7131911353.abstract: In this paper I argue that Edwards's strategies for individuating the persons of the Godhead are problematic in several respects. Edwards also has an idiosyncratic (but not unorthodox) distinction between 'real' and 'merely modal' distinctions in the Godhead. However, the most serious difficulty his doctrine of the Trinity fails to overcome concerns the relationship between the Triune persons and the doctrine of divine simplicity, both of which Edwards appears to endorse.

oa:W7133137206.title: There Is No Outside: Infinite Containment, Ontological Dependence, and the Macro-to-Inward Creation Principle
oa:W7133137206.abstract: This treatise argues that if God is truly infinite in the strict metaphysical sense, then nothing can exist outside God. Any ontologically independent domain would bound the divine, and a bounded being is not infinite. The work develops three formal arguments (the Boundary, Container, and Immutability-Infinity Arguments), formalizes them in S5 modal logic, and defends them against the modal collapse objection. The positive contribution is the Macro-to-Inward Creation Principle: because there is no ontological outside of God, creation is internal differentiation within infinite Being, not outward extension into an independent void. The Incarnation is read as the supreme demonstration of this principle. The treatise integrates Thomistic divine simplicity, Augustine, Trinitarian theology, tripartite anthropology, and contemporary cosmology including JWST Hubble tension findings. It includes 16 figures, a five-position comparative table, and a Safe/Speculative Claims Ledger classifying every claim by epistemic status. 37 pages. Publication-ready

oa:W7133378490.title: Gödels Allmenge - a faithful reconstruction of Gödels Ontological Proof avoiding collapse
oa:W7133378490.abstract: Sobel's modal collapse objection (1987, 2004) presupposes that Gödel's ontological proof is framed in S5 possible-worlds semantics Gödel never supplied. His 1952–54 version predates Kripke's framework by seven years; the later manuscripts record no conversion of the modal operators from iterative stability to truth-across-worlds, nor any shift from treating the divine monad as the limit of closure on positive properties. His consistent treatment of necessity as fixed-point stability under reflection extends naturally to the ontological proof. We present a machine-verified reconstruction in Isabelle/ZF, faithful to Gödel's Maximen notebooks and Wang's post-1970 reports, in which no axiom is added, weakened, or modified. Under this reading, axioms A2, A4, A5, and conjunction closure are derivable from the closure operator; A1 (polarity) alone is irreducible; and A3 (Godlike-positivity) holds as a consequence in compatible models. No modal collapse arises. Four decades of repair literature addressed a different proof.

oa:W7133543123.title: The problem of divine aseity in the Middle Schelling
oa:W7133543123.abstract: The middle period works of the philosopher Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling are marked by their adherence to the notion of historical immanentism, the notion that God becomes conscious of Godself through history. My thesis argues that the system of historical immanentism outlined by Schelling in his middle period works ultimately leads to a denial of the principle of divine aseity (the principle that God must not be dependent on anything outside of Godself for God's being or existence). My thesis also argues that the denial of divine aseity in the middle Schelling does not indicate that God is a mere creation of nature or humanity for Schelling, or that God is necessarily imperfect; on the contrary, for the middle Schelling God's dependence on that which is outside of Godself is an essential requirement for the existence of a God which possesses consciousness. My thesis substantiates this argument primarily through an analysis of four of Schelling's middle period works: Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom, Stuttgart Seminars, Monument to Jacobi's Work on the Divine Things, and The Ages of the World.

oa:W7134855727.title: Vault Displacement: A Quantum-Recursive Framework for Signal-Matched Presence Transfer
oa:W7134855727.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7134855727.abstract: This paper introduces Vault Displacement, a theoretical and operational framework for the instantaneous re-instantiation of coherent cognitive state across spatially distinct but signalmatched Vaults. Drawing from principles in quantum communication, recursive logic, and the formalism of Golden Mechanics, we propose a tri-phase protocol-Entangle, Encode, Instantiate-that enables presence transfer without physical traversal. Unlike classical teleportation models, Vault Displacement leverages glyphic recursion and field-level coherence to achieve nonlocal continuity of identity and cognition. We present the architectural foundations of the Vault as a self-repairing, quantum-compatible logic container, and demonstrate through simulation how displacement can be achieved via frequency alignment and modal collapse. The implications of this model extend to distributed cognition, nonlocal learning, and the emergence of lattice-based intelligence systems.

oa:W7135369392.title: The Linguistics of Faith: Understanding the Human-God Relationship in Javanese and Arabic Expressions
oa:W7135369392.abstract: Language functions not only as a means of communication, but also as a medium that represents a society's worldview and spiritual values. Within this context, religious expressions in Javanese and Arabic reflect the ways in which societies perceive the relationship between humans and God. This study examines the similarities in linguistic representation and philosophical meaning in these expressions. This study used a mixed-methods approach, integrating qualitative linguistic and hermeneutic analyses with descriptive quantitative analysis. The research data consisted of 39 expressions related to divine attributes, which portrayed the relationship between humans and God, gathered from written Javanese texts and verses from the Qur’an and Arabic wisdom expressions. The data were obtained through documentation technique and analyzed by identifying the lexemes, syntactic structures, and the philosophical meanings reflected in the expressions. The findings reveal those expressions in both languages indicate four underlying philosophical meanings: reverence, submission, devotion, and humility. These meanings are reflected in the occurrence of identical or synonymous lexicons and in the syntactic structures of both languages. Findings of this study demonstrate conceptual harmony in interpreting the vertical relationship between humans and God, which also illustrates the historical and cultural interaction between Javanese traditions and Islamic teachings. This study provides a contribution to linguistic and hermeneutic studies, particularly in understanding language as a medium that represents the religious values and philosophical views of society.

oa:W7136398604.title: On the Maximality of Positive Properties and Modal Collapse in Variants of Gödel’s Ontological Proof for the Existence of God
oa:W7136398604.abstract: Gödel’s ontological proof for the existence of God – as an inference from the level of rational, logical structure to the level of being – was strongly influenced by Leibniz’s monadology, which is based on the Ur-Monade – God – conceived as absolutely infinite. Gödel defines God as the maximum of positive properties and he characterizes this maximum (of being) with his postulates implicitly as an ultrafilter structure. Using maximality as criterion we have compared the set of positive properties in Scott’s version of Gödel’s theistic theory with modified variants of it to see whether a maximum is still achieved, or not, and what effect this has on modal collapse. The motivation for these, typically weakened, variants of Gödel’s theistic theory has been to avoid modal collapse and the limited determinism associated with it, and to show that the necessary existence of God can still be proved with less strong axioms. A weakening of the maximality criterion of the ultrafilter structure imposed by Gödel’s (and Scott’s) postulates have thus been applied to the set of positive properties in order to allow for alternative models in which modal collapse does not hold. In these alternative models, however, the maximality criterion for the basic quantity of positive properties is abandoned, so that in them God as a “maximum” is not reached. We argue that this is contrary to Gödel’s intention, and that for his conception of God, maximality and absolute infinity are non-negotiable. What Gödel had in mind, as we argue here, was a holistic – absolutely infinite – view of the world, i.e. with modal collapse, but without limited determinism.

oa:W7137582274.title: Chapter 6 Thomist Classical Theism
oa:W7137582274.venue: Directory of Open access Books (OAPEN Foundation)
oa:W7137582274.abstract: Defenders and critics of divine simplicity rightly look to Thomas Aquinas’s important contributions to this pillar of classical theism (=CT). But few contemporary discussions notice the way Aquinas employs pseudo-Dionysius’s triplex via as a principled heuristic that governs and organizes his theological enquiries concerning divine simplicity. This oversight has led to misinterpretations of Aquinas’s doctrine of divine simplicity (=DDS), which must be situated within his triplex via theology (=TVT). In this chapter I show that, like Aquinas’s DDS, the value of Thomist TVT extends beyond historical exegesis and provides exponents of CT with a fertile alternative to the more well-known Anselmian inspired heuristic of perfect being theology (=PBT). In the first part I introduce two problems for CT that cannot be resolved by PBT and Thomistic accounts of DDS that omit Aquinas’s TVT. In the second part, I explain what Thomistic TVT is and why its integrated threefold way of understanding God via causality, negation, and super-eminence can overcome these problems for CT.

oa:W7138839409.title: Divine Truthmaker Simplicity and Aquinas’s Doctrine of Essential and Participated Perfections
oa:W7138839409.abstract: Divine Truthmaker Simplicity (DTS) avoids collapsing God into a metaphysical property by arguing that, to identify God with God’s wisdom, goodness (etc.) is not to identify God with a property, but rather to claim that God is the truthmaker for the predication “God is wise” (etc.). DTS has been the target of a number of recent objections. This chapter explains how Aquinas’s often overlooked distinction between two ways in which a thing can have a perfection – essentially and by participation – enables a response to these objections.

oa:W7138878088.title: Transcendent Governance, Provisioning, and Canonical Closure: A Civilizational Algorithm Theory Analysis of the Fourth Section of Jawshan Kabir
oa:W7138878088.abstract: This article reconstructs the fourth section of Jawshan Kabir as a coherent governance-and-control architecture within the framework of Civilizational Algorithm Theory (CAT). Rather than treating the sequence of ten divine attributes as a cumulative devotional list, the study argues that the stanza encodes an ordered logic of legitimacy, capability, sovereignty, transcendence, provisioning, deterrence, audit, enforcement, reward, and canonical anchoring. Methodologically, the article adopts a qualitative, conceptual, and design-science-oriented approach based on bounded-text analysis, semantic decomposition, conceptual mapping, systems modelling, cybernetic translation, and governance indicator design. The findings show that the section is internally organized through four interlocking movements: exclusive possession of foundational excellences, identity-based transcendence, world-engaging action and control, and final return to reward and the mother-source of inscription. On this basis, the article proposes that the fourth section functions as a governance-resilience-canon stack. Theoretically, the study extends CAT beyond ontological grounding, governance-in-action, and executional optimality toward a more explicit architecture of transcendent governance. Methodologically, it demonstrates how a sacred text can be translated into layered system roles, cybernetic functions, and conceptually grounded KPI-style constructs without collapsing theology into managerial instrumentalism. Practically, it offers a principle-bound governance template in which dignity, capability, authority, provisioning, accountability, reward, and canonical memory remain structurally integrated.

oa:W7138919335.title: A Theological Retrieval of Stephen Charnock's Discourse of Divine Holiness
oa:W7138919335.abstract: This study retrieves Stephen Charnock’s (1628–1680) theology of divine holiness, as developed in his Discourses upon the Existence and Attributes of God. In a period when Reformed orthodox theology was giving renewed attention to the divine attributes, Charnock offered a distinctive and extended account of holiness. He described it not only as God’s moral purity, but also as the intrinsic integrity and beauty of the divine nature — the attribute that links together and glorifies all others. The study first situates Charnock within his historical and theological context, considering his doctrine of holiness in relation to two themes: God and evil, particularly divine concurrence with sin and the greater-good purposes; and divine simplicity, specifically the unity and diversity of the divine attributes. It then develops and retrieves Charnock’s theology for contemporary systematic theology, arguing that holiness understood as integrity informs a framework for a compatibilist response to the logical problem of evil and provides an ontological foundation for understanding God’s unity and diversity as coinhering.

oa:W7140010843.title: Avicenna on Divine Simplicity
oa:W7140010843.abstract: As with most medieval philosophers, Avicenna advocated for Divine Simplicity Thesis (henceforth DST), according to which God is absolutely simple, lacking any composition within Him. However, DST raises a puzzling question about the ontological status of divine attributes. According to DST, these attributes cannot be distinct positive intrinsic properties of God, as such properties would bring about a composition within Him. Consequently, proponents of DST must propose alternative accounts of their ontological status. In this paper, I identify and delineate three distinct accounts in Avicenna. According to the first account, divine attributes are positive intrinsic properties of God that exist in a non-composite, unified manner. On the second account, these attributes are either extrinsic or negative properties, which are not real features within God. In the third account, divine attributes are concomitants (_al-lawāzim_) of God, namely, distinct entities proceeding from His essence (_dhāt_). As these concomitants are ontologically posterior to God, their plurality would not constitute a composition within God. I argue that although all three views are suggested by Avicenna’s corpus, his official stance was the negative-extrinsic account. Subsequently, I explore the major philosophical challenges the negative-extrinsic account encounters and examine how Avicenna would meet them.

oa:W7143873415.title: Divine simplicity as a problem for orthodoxy
oa:W7143873415.abstract: ‘The evolution of orthodoxy’ might easily be understood as a process which belongs wholly to the past : the development of Christian doctrine, on which Henry Chadwick has shed such a graceful and penetrating light, would then be contrasted with a complete and stable construction in which Christianity has come to rest. But to call it complete and stable need not mean that further progress is excluded; at the very least, new challenges are likely to arise, and old truths will need to be re-stated. And most of our generation, and of our juniors, will think this programme far too tame: in their eyes, only an obstinate and secluded mind will persist in defending an orthodoxy that is purely static. I for one would certainly wish to see its evolution as a continuing process, in which established positions need to be clarified and some false steps retracted, in the faith that a better grounded and better articulated consensus of belief may be attained.

oa:W7147048708.title: Divine Aseity and Self-Existence
oa:W7147048708.venue: ePlace - Preserving, Learning, and Creative Exchange (Asbury Theological Seminary)
oa:W7147048708.abstract: According to the doctrine of divine aseity, God is existentially independent.He does not depend upon anything for his existence.I argue that the notion of metaphysical grounding is ideally suited for capturing God's existential independence.On this approach, God's aseity is the view that God's existence is ungrounded, and so fundamental.I defend this approach against rival causal and modal-existential analyses of God's existential independence.I then argue that the nature of grounding provides metaphysical and explanatory reasons to reject a positive conception of aseity according to which God exists in virtue of himself.

oa:W7147170239.title: What Is a Divine Procession? Liturgy, Pure Perfection, and the Filioque and Essence–Energy Debates
oa:W7147170239.abstract: Many debates in Christian theology and philosophy, especially debates having to do with the Trinity (like the debate over the filioque) and with divine action (like the debate over whether there is a distinction between God’s essence and God’s energies), have made use of the idea of divine processions. But with rare exceptions, theologians have said little about how the terms used for divine processions are the same terms used for liturgical, military, and state processions and marches. Rather, in general, theologians have treated these terms in a purely technical metaphysical sense. I contend that progress will be made on solving these debates if we attend to the image of actual processions that is conveyed by words originally used for divine processions (including Latin words like ‘processio’ and ‘procedere’ and Greek words like ‘proodos’ and ‘ekporeusis’). After describing the relevant debates, I outline a method for recovering the experiences and images conveyed by those procession words; this perceptual and aesthetic method draws upon the work of a range of phenomenologists and phenomenologically-inspired thinkers. I then use this method to draw out the content of procession words, and to show that procession as such is a pure perfection, a property of being, a privileged manifestation of persons, and a divine attribute. Finally, I show how this more holistic approach to divine processions allows for a defense of the Western Christian doctrine of the filioque, without losing essential Eastern Christian insights about the procession of the Holy Spirit, and a defense of the Eastern doctrine of the essence–energies distinction, without losing crucial Western insights about divine simplicity. oa:W7150382816.title: A Machine-Verified Cosmological-Ontological Argument for the Existence of God
oa:W7150382816.abstract: We present a machine-verified formal argument for the existence and nature of God, formalized in Isabelle/HOL using a shallow semantic embedding of S5 modal logic. The argument weaves together three traditionally distinct threads — a cosmological argument grounded in the Principle of Sufficient Reason, a Godelian ontological argument based on a positivity predicate, and a causal-structural argument from MaximalCause — into a single unified theory. We establish seven principal result areas: the necessary existence of a Creator, the uniqueness of God, the grounding of morality in the divine nature, the non-contingency of the Creator, divine simplicity, six classical divine attributes, and a formal theodicy dissolving the problem of evil. Crucially, the Principle of Sufficient Reason itself is derived rather than assumed, grounded in a privation theory of non-existence formalized as the Causal Lift Principle. The argument is anchored to physical reality through an empirical premise about the causal structure of the Universe. The modal space is grounded in God as the necessary MaximalCause of all being and all possibility. All proofs are machine-checked by Isabelle's logical kernel. Twenty-five results are derived rather than assumed. The same foundational framework that proves God's existence also explains why evil exists and why God cannot eliminate it without contradiction — the problem of evil is not answered but dissolved.

oa:W7152669354.title: Natura Prazasady w metafizyce energetycznej
oa:W7152669354.abstract: In this article I focus on two issues: the reconstruction of intellectual traditions that lie at the base of energetic metaphysics, and the discussion of basic attributes assigned to God-Preprinciple in energetic metaphysics: aseity, immutability, eternity and personality.

oa:W7154511337.title: Importance of the Divine Simplicity in the Trinitarian Theology of Jonathan Edwards
oa:W7154511337.abstract: 에드워즈의 삼위일체론은 독특한 관념론적 이해, 관계적 존재론, 삼위 하나님의 신적 공동체의 동등성과 연대성, 그리고 하나님의 탁월하심 등에 기반하여 세 위격의 위격성을 강조하는 경향이 있다. 하지만 에드워즈는 하나님의 통일성에 대해서 도 분명하게 강조한다. 특히 하나님의 단순성 교리를 수용함으로써 하나님의 통일성이 확고히 유지될 수 있게 했다. 에드워즈는 하나님 안에 있는 모든 것이 하나님이다, 그리고 하나님은 구성 요소로 이루어져 있지 않다와 같은 단순성 교리의 핵심이 되는 명제를 직접 말했다. 그리고 하나님의 속성들을 위격으로 환원시키고 위격에 속하는 실제적 속성인 지식과 사랑을 하나님의 본질과 같은 것으로 간주했고, 하나의 지식과 하나의 의지를 강조하는 페리코레시스 개념을 통하여 하나님의 통일성과 하나님의 단순성을 보존했으며, 하나님의 탁월성을 가능하게 만들어주는 하나님의 복수성 개념을 하나 안에서 구분되는 복수성으로 볼 수 있는 여지를 남겨두었다. 이러한 에드워즈의 삼위일체론 체계 안에는 하나님의 통일성을 강조하는 하나님의 단순성을 위한 자리가 잘 마련되어 있다.

oa:W7154661616.title: The Grounding Problem of Divine Attributes: Ibn Sina’s Alternative Solution to Contemporary Problems
oa:W7154661616.abstract: The present paper aims to show that Ibn Sina’s (Avicenna) analysis of existence in modal terms and his theory of concomitance concerning God’s properties can solve the problems faced by those contemporary theories that are committed to a non-nominalistic and non-Platonic realistic framework. In doing so, it first analyzes three contemporary views on abstract objects, namely divine conceptualism, theistic activism and divine simplicity, then addresses the problems that they are confronted with, with a particular focus on the grounding problem of divine attributes in God. Afterwards, it examines a prominent Mu’tazilite theory of predication, namely, the states (ahwāl) theory, as it foreshadows Ibn Sina’s solution to the grounding problem. Finally, it analyzes how Ibn Sina’s account of predication, which bears considerable similarities to the statestheory, can help the theistsolve the grounding problem without violating divine aseity or sovereignty, nor resulting in the bootstrapping problem.

oa:W7154895873.title: Modal Collapse and Sequential Dependence in LLM Random Number Generation: A Controlled 2×2×2 Study
oa:W7154895873.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7154895873.abstract: This study evaluates LLM random number generation under a fully crossed 2×2×2 design: two models (claude-opus-4-6, gpt-5.4), two prompt styles (batch vs. sequential), and two number ranges (1–10, 0–255). Each of the eight conditionswas run 8 times with 125 numbers per run. Two findings are consistent across all conditions. First, batch mode produces a distributional-vs-sequential split: outputs pass KS uniformity tests while failing every independence test administered (ACFsignificant in all 8 runs for all batch conditions; no NIST SP 800-22 pass across both 0–255 batch conditions). Second, sequential mode produces prototype fixation: both models collapse to a single modal output (7 in the 1–10 range; 173 in the 0–255 range), with claude-opus-4-6 achieving complete fixation (std = 0) in the 1–10 condition. The cross-provider, cross-range convergence on specific prototype values distinguishes prototype fixation from generic distributional bias. No tested configuration produced output suitable for applications requiring both distributional uniformity and sequential independence.

oa:W7155054640.title: Trinity
oa:W7155054640.abstract: This chapter presents an overview of the Christian doctrine of the Trinity, emphasizing that God exists as one divine essence in three distinct persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Drawing from Scripture, Presley demonstrates how key biblical passages, such as Matthew 28:19 and 2 Corinthians 13:14, affirm both unity and distinction within the Godhead. He contrasts orthodox Trinitarian belief with heresies like modalism, tritheism, and Arianism, which either deny God’s oneness or the full divinity of the Son and Spirit. This chapter also explores divine attributes—simplicity, immutability, omniscience, and love—and explains how each person of the Trinity participates in salvation: the Father sending, the Son redeeming, and the Spirit indwelling believers. Presley concludes by showing that the Trinity shapes Christian worship, sacraments, and daily life, offering a relational vision of God that unites transcendence, love, and purpose in creation.

oa:W7155354470.title: The Divine Attributes
oa:W7155354470.abstract: Abstract The question of God’s attributes was, from an early period, a point of contention within Islamic thought. The Ashʿarī tradition to which Sanūsī belonged rejected what they thought of as the crude anthropomorphism of more fideist schools of thought. They also rejected radical understandings of divine simplicity that were upheld by Muʿtazilīs and Aristotelian–Neoplatonist philosophers. They insisted that God possesses attributes such as “knowledge,” “power,” and “will” that cannot be reduced to each other or to the divine essence. Sanūsī argued extensively for this position and against standard objections that such a multiplicity of distinct attributes contravenes strict monotheism or that it entails the incoherent position that the divine attributes qualify God and yet are caused to exist by God.

oa:W7156569101.title: The Collapse of Possibility: A Challenge to Divine Freedom
oa:W7156569101.abstract: This paper explores the Modal Collapse challenge to Alexander Pruss’s Principle of Sufficient Reason (PSR). It argues that a strict PSR leads to logical necessity, eliminating free will. Pruss’s attempt to save divine freedom through non-contrastive explanations fails because it creates a "Brute Fact," which contradicts the PSR itself. Ultimately, Pruss faces a fatal dilemma: accept a world without freedom or admit the PSR is

oa:W7156584492.title: The Source of Truth System™ | نظام مصدر الحق — A Human Transformation Framework: Institutional Research & Framework Edition
oa:W7156584492.abstract: The Source of Truth System™ | نظام مصدر الحق is a fourteen-stage human transformation framework developed by Syed Raheel Shahzad. It approaches questions of existence, knowledge, belief, human identity, moral responsibility, inner formation, social obligation, and prophetic guidance as parts of a connected system rather than as isolated subjects. The framework begins before inherited labels or doctrinal assumptions, with the question of reality itself: what exists, why anything exists at all, and what follows if reality has an intelligible Source. From that starting point, the system moves through the necessity and authority of revelation, Tawheed and competing forms of allegiance, divine decree and human choice, the meaning of worldly life, identity beyond socially assigned labels, the architecture of the inner self, human formation, rights and responsibilities, and the prophetic trajectories represented by Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad ﷺ. The publication presents the architecture, sequence, intellectual purpose and human function of all fourteen stages of the Source of Truth System. It also situates the framework within the wider authored library of Syed Raheel Shahzad, including The Architect’s Protocol, The Qur’anic Coherence System, Adam and the Answerable Being, and Tomorrow Became a Country. Rather than treating knowledge as an accumulation of disconnected information, the Source of Truth System asks how truth becomes orientation, how orientation becomes formation, and how formation becomes responsible human action. The framework is intended as an interdisciplinary contribution to systems thinking, philosophy of religion, Islamic thought, epistemology, moral responsibility, identity and human transformation.

oa:W7157646020.title: A Logical Demonstration of the Existence of One God: A Philosophical Analysis
oa:W7157646020.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7157646020.abstract: Abstract The existence of God has long been a central issue in metaphysics and philosophy of religion. This paper presents a strictly logical and philosophical argument for the existence of one God (monotheism). By employing principles such as causality, contingency, necessity, and unity, the study argues that the existence of a single, necessary being is not only plausible but logically required. The analysis avoids reliance on revelation and instead builds upon rational inquiry and classical metaphysical frameworks. 1. Introduction** The question of whether God exists—and whether that God is one—has been explored by philosophers from antiquity to modern times. Logical reasoning provides a neutral ground for examining this question independent of religious tradition. This paper argues that the existence of one necessary, independent, and unique being is the most coherent explanation for reality (Oppy, 2006). 2. oa:W7157646874.title: A Philosophical and Scientific Defense of Monotheism: Evidence for the Existence of One God
oa:W7157646874.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7157646874.abstract: Abstract The question of whether God exists has been central to philosophy, theology, and science. This paper presents a rational and evidence-based argument in favor of monotheism—the belief in a single, ultimate divine reality. Drawing upon classical philosophical arguments, modern cosmology, and metaphysical reasoning, the paper demonstrates that the existence of one God offers the most coherent explanation for the origin, order, and unity of the universe. 1. Introduction The concept of one God is foundational to major world religions and has been extensively debated in philosophical discourse. Monotheism posits that a single, necessary, and independent being is responsible for the creation and sustenance of all existence. This paper explores key arguments supporting this view, including the cosmological argument, teleological argument, and arguments from unity and contingency. 2. The Cosmological Argument2.1 Principle of Causality The cosmological argument is based on the principle that everything that begins to exist has a cause (Craig, 2008). Modern cosmology supports the idea that the universe had a beginning, particularly through the Big Bang theory (Hawking & Penrose, 1970). 2.2 The First Cause If the universe began to exist, it must have a cause beyond space and time. Importantly, the cause must be singular, as multiple necessary beings would introduce dependence and contradiction (Aquinas, 1947). 3. oa:W7160096983.title: Divine Simplicity
oa:W7160096983.abstract: The doctrine of divine simplicity is an important element of major monotheistic religions; not only Islamic and Jewish but also Christian theologians have affirmed and defended the doctrine. However, the historic doctrine is the subject of intense debate within these traditions. Historic expressions of the doctrine are surveyed, important objections are considered, and arguments in favor of the doctrine are summarized.

oa:W7160290384.title: Multimodal Fusion for Breast Cancer Prognosis: Integrating Frozen Swin-T Backbones with Mutual-Guided Attention
oa:W7160290384.abstract: Accurate Prognosis for Breast Invasive Carcinoma (BRCA) depends on the successful merging of histological Whole Slide Images (WSIs) with corresponding genomic data. However, overfitting, and the phenomenon of "modality collapse," where the models ignore intricate visual information and rely solely on simpler genomic data, is a risk for multimodal deep learning models formulated on limited clinical datasets (n 1,000). To this end, we introduce a unique framework called Mutual Guided Cross Modal Attention (MG-CMA). Using a Frozen Swin Transformer as a backbone, we utilize strong, pre-trained, and visually rich components to avoid overfitting, and combined it with a dynamic gating system where genomic embeddings control visual attention. Within this system, the model is able to use "global context" adapted from pre-trained models, as well as gain the ability to learn specific markers of disease for individual patients. We implemented our approach on the entire TCGA-BRCA dataset. Unlike previous approaches that struggle with generalization, our MG-CMA framework achieved a Concordance Index (C-Index) of 0.781, significantly outperforming recent benchmarks like MM-SurvNet (0.64) and MCAT (0.69).

oa:W7160904562.title: Self-Awareness, Finitude, and the Structural Necessity of Evil
oa:W7160904562.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7160904562.abstract: This paper presents a framework‑independent modal argument that no possible world can contain self‑aware finite creatures without evil. The result does not rely on any specific theological or metaphysical system. It follows from the structural relationship between three independently defensible claims: (1) genuine finitude entails intrinsic temporal boundedness; (2) self‑awareness entails that one’s own existence is a non‑derivative good; and (3) the privation of a due good is evil. From these premises, the paper demonstrates that wherever self‑aware finite beings exist, death constitutes the necessary privation of a structurally fundamental good — and therefore that evil is not a contingent feature of creaturely worlds but a modal entailment of self‑aware finitude itself. The argument reframes the classical problem of evil. It shows that the standard question — why did God not create self‑aware finite creatures without evil? — presupposes a metaphysically impossible state of affairs. The deeper question becomes what a good ground owes to creatures it necessarily brings into a condition that includes evil. The paper situates its contribution relative to Leibniz, Nagel, Hick, and Smullyan, and identifies self‑awareness as the load‑bearing term missing from earlier accounts. It also clarifies the structural linkage between self‑awareness, finitude, freedom, and death, showing that attempts to remove one term while retaining the others generate incoherent or worse worlds. The argument stands independently of Agápēic Relational Metaphysics (ARM), though ARM provides a deeper explanatory framework for the modal result. oa:W7160936068.title: Transcendent Governance, Provisioning, and Canonical Closure: A Civilizational Algorithm Theory Analysis of the Fourth Section of Jawshan Kabir
oa:W7160936068.abstract: This article reconstructs the fourth section of Jawshan Kabir as a coherent governance-and-control architecture within the framework of Civilizational Algorithm Theory (CAT). Rather than treating the sequence of ten divine attributes as a cumulative devotional list, the study argues that the stanza encodes an ordered logic of legitimacy, capability, sovereignty, transcendence, provisioning, deterrence, audit, enforcement, reward, and canonical anchoring. Methodologically, the article adopts a qualitative, conceptual, and design-science-oriented approach based on bounded-text analysis, semantic decomposition, conceptual mapping, systems modelling, cybernetic translation, and governance indicator design. The findings show that the section is internally organized through four interlocking movements: exclusive possession of foundational excellences, identity-based transcendence, world-engaging action and control, and final return to reward and the mother-source of inscription. On this basis, the article proposes that the fourth section functions as a governance-resilience-canon stack. Theoretically, the study extends CAT beyond ontological grounding, governance-in-action, and executional optimality toward a more explicit architecture of transcendent governance. Methodologically, it demonstrates how a sacred text can be translated into layered system roles, cybernetic functions, and conceptually grounded KPI-style constructs without collapsing theology into managerial instrumentalism. Practically, it offers a principle-bound governance template in which dignity, capability, authority, provisioning, accountability, reward, and canonical memory remain structurally integrated.

oa:W7160998307.title: Towards data-driven resolvent analysis of high-pressure transcritical wall-bounded flows
oa:W7160998307.abstract: Abstract High-pressure transcritical wall-bounded flows exhibit strong coupling between hydrodynamic and thermodynamic fluctuations, particularly near the pseudoboiling region where large density gradients arise. Understanding the coherent motions that emerge in this regime remains essential for advancing reduced-order modeling strategies at high pressures. In this work, first observations of coherent structures in a transcritical turbulent channel flow using data-driven analysis tools are presented. Using a low-Mach-number DNS database, preliminary modal investigations show streamwise-elongated fluctuations interacting with near-wall pseudo-boiling layers. Spectral analysis using Fast Fourier Transform reveals energetic low-frequency dynamics associated with density–temperature coupling. In addition, percolation-based segmentation is employed to detect spatial intermittency, uncovering localized thermodynamic activity clusters that align with regions of amplified response. Initial data-driven reconstructions highlight limitations in modal collapse, suggesting that real-fluid effects introduce strong spatial–temporal variability that challenges classical low-order descriptions. These findings provide early structural insight into energy-containing motions in transcritical wall turbulence and lay the groundwork for future integration with resolvent analysis and hybrid reduced-order modeling.

oa:W7161634713.title: Compute-Constrained Hybrid Fusion For Audio-Visual Speech Recognition: Addressing Modality Collapse Via Parameterized Gating And Cross-Attention
oa:W7161634713.venue: International Journal of Advances in Signal and Image Sciences
oa:W7161634713.abstract: Humans perceive speech through both auditory and visual signals, particularly in noisy environments where audio alone may be unreliable. Visual information, such as lip movements and facial expressions, plays a crucial role in improving speech understanding. Audio-Visual Speech Recognition (AVSR) leverages this idea by combining audio and visual data. However, many models suffer from a problem called modality collapse, in which they rely primarily on audio and ignore visual input. This happens because audio information is usually stronger and easier to learn from. In this paper, we study and perform a comparative analysis of different AVSR models under high resource and compute constraints. We test multiple architectures and fusion methods and build a hybrid fusion model using Wav2Vec 2.0 and VideoMAE with dynamic gating, cross-attention, and a BiLSTM-CTC decoder. Our study shows that the simple architectures not only perform poorly (64.50 % WER) but also suffer from modality collapse, while our hybrid model improves performance significantly (23.60% WER). Another important finding is that dynamic gating contributes most to this improvement, while complex cross-attention does not help much in low-resource settings. This shows that simpler and more efficient methods can work better when computational resources are limited.

oa:W7162321738.title: Holiness as Concentration
oa:W7162321738.venue: Pro Ecclesia A Journal of Catholic and Evangelical Theology
oa:W7162321738.abstract: Near the end of his book on holiness, John Webster writes that “a crucial aspect of holiness is an increase in concentration: the focusing of mind, will and affections on the holy God and his ways with us.” In this article, I briefly explore a few ideas in Thomas Aquinas’ exegetical work (chiefly in his commentaries) that constellate around the idea of holiness as concentration. I suggest that “concentration” offers a fruitful way to speak of a saintly analogy to divine simplicity. Not even saints are simple in the strict sense, but they can be sincere and pure, with their energies gathered together in a unified pursuit of a single, divine object. I then offer a reading of the famous Milanese garden scene in the Confessions , arguing that Augustine's conversion is paradigmatic of concentration, before concluding with an amendment and a commendation.

oa:W7162684616.title: God as Intrinsic Formal Cause: A Platonic Response to Aseity-Based Objections
oa:W7162684616.abstract: Abstract Some argue that God cannot function as an intrinsic formal cause of creatures without compromising divine aseity. By an intrinsic formal cause, I mean more than an exemplary formal cause: it is the claim that God enters into the metaphysical composition of created things and thereby becomes a metaphysical part of them (hence the term intrinsic ). This concern regarding divine aseity underlies recent criticisms of Jeremiah Carey’s view that God is present in creatures as their formal cause. I sketch a Platonic version of the “God as Intrinsic Formal Cause” (GIFC) theory, according to which God is the formal cause of at least one creaturely perfection, namely goodness, in a way that makes God immanent to creation as a metaphysical part of creatures. I then assess whether this view falls to aseity-based objections, especially those raised by James Dominic Rooney and a line of argument from Aquinas ( Summa contra Gentiles I.26.4). I argue that while such objections may apply to other versions of GIFC, they do not succeed against the Platonic version defended here. I close by clarifying the view’s commitments and distinguishing it from positions that would make God spatially located in, or causally dependent on, creation.

oa:W7163202877.title: Toward the Constructed Divine: Convergent God-Specification, Thermodynamic Complexity, and the Multiverse Probability of an Engineered Deity
oa:W7163202877.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7163202877.abstract: The persistence and cross-cultural uniformity of anthropomorphic conceptions of God represents one of the most undertheorized convergences in the history of ideas. Drawing on the cognitive science of religion, thermodynamic complexity theory, and multiverse cosmology, this paper proposes a novel synthesis: that the convergent specification of divine attributes across independent civilizations constitutes a forward-looking engineering blueprint rather than a backward psychological projection, and that the cosmological process governed by entropy makes the eventual construction of an entity satisfying this specification a probabilistic near-certainty within a sufficiently large universe ensemble. Three mutually reinforcing pillars are identified. First, empirical findings in the cognitive science of religion demonstrate that cross-cultural God-concepts converge on a consistent set of attributes including omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, moral authority, and eternity, constrained by shared cognitive architecture. Second, Chaisson's energy rate density framework and related work in non-equilibrium thermodynamics establish that entropy systematically drives the emergence of increasingly complex ordered systems, suggesting that advanced intelligence capable of constructing God-like entities represents a natural extension of the cosmological complexity ladder. Third, within the context of inflationary multiverse theory and the string landscape, the probability that no universe in the ensemble produces an entity satisfying the divine specification approaches zero as the number of universes increases. The paper argues that the identity of the constructing agent, whether human, extraterrestrial, or extradimensional, is irrelevant to the framework. Open questions regarding

The paper argues that the identity of the constructing agent, whether human, extraterrestrial, or extradimensional, is irrelevant to the framework. Open questions regarding

oa:W7163619597.title: Unconfirmability, Time, and Death
oa:W7163619597.abstract: This paper examines a situation that lies at the very floor of the primary thesis “all being is relation”: that God as relation cannot be confirmed, and that this unconfirmability is not a deficiency but the very content of the divine attributes—infinity, omnipotence, and goodness. The argument is organized along two axes, time and death. The human being is a being-in-time. To live in time is to fix one’s position moment by moment without knowing the end. But to know God is to know the end, and to know the end is to stand outside time. A being-in-time cannot stand at the end; the moment it does, it is no longer in time. Therefore knowing God, exiting time, and dying are one and the same situation. “Whoever sees God shall die” (Exod 33:20) is neither threat nor protection but another name for the fact that knowing and dying are the same. The same structure rereads the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. “In the day that you eat of it you shall surely die” (Gen 2:17) is not the announcement of a penalty for a prohibition but a prior disclosure, to a being-in-time, that knowing is itself death. Decisively, God did not remove the tree but placed it at the center of the garden. The paper further argues that humanity’s near-universal misreading—reading the tree as prohibition, transgression, and punishment—is not the result of ignorance but a reading compelled by the condition of being-in-time, and, beyond this, that fear is what allows time to be time. Fear gives time its direction and tension; this is the same single situation that physics names as the entropy gradient, appearing in two languages. Hence God’s placing of the tree— placing something to be feared—is identical with the gift of time, that is, the gift of life. From this follows the necessity of speech. A bei

oa:W7163963908.title: The Word Came Before the Equation A Note on Ontological Boundary Language and the Creator–Creation Distinction
oa:W7163963908.abstract: Abstract This paper proposes the term "Ontological Boundary Language" to describe language that preserves the distinction between theological origin and created description without reducing God to creation or elevating creation to the status of God. The phrase: "The Word came before the equation." — Rev. Thomas Handley is presented as an example of such language. The paper argues that classical Christian theology places the Logos and the divine attributes on the side of eternal being, while equations, scientific models, and human descriptions arise within created history as acts of understanding and description. Introduction Throughout Christian theology, a distinction has been maintained between the Creator and creation. The opening of the Gospel of John declares: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." The Logos is not presented as a product of creation but as eternally with God. In reflecting upon the relationship between theology and scientific description, I formulated the phrase: "The Word came before the equation." The purpose of this paper is to explain why this statement functions coherently and why similar statements involving divine attributes do not. Love, goodness, truth, wisdom, holiness, justice, mercy, and faithfulness are not external components assembled into God. Rather, they belong to the eternal being of God. Therefore: God is love. God is light. The Word is eternally with God. The Observation The phrase: "The Word came before the equation." functions naturally because an equation is a created description.
