oa:W7164156925.title: The Terminus Problem: Constitutive Necessity and the Aseity of the Agápēic Ground
oa:W7164156925.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7164156925.abstract: This paper introduces a third structural profile in the divine aseity debate — constitutive necessity — that occupies the space between self-grounding and brute fundamentality, and argues that it is the only profile that genuinely closes the terminus problem rather than relocating or abandoning it. The paper accepts Oberle's recent argument (Faith and Philosophy, 2026) that positive aseity is incoherent given the irreflexivity of grounding, and then presses the question his account leaves open: if brute negative aseity is the only remaining option, has philosophy answered the terminus question or merely abandoned it? The answer defended here is that brute negative aseity fails on its own terms — it stops the explanatory regress by declaration rather than by structural completion, and cannot explain why the terminus is generative rather than inert, or why the regress stops here rather than at a simpler or different candidate. Constitutive necessity is the alternative: a structure whose co-actuality follows from what each internal role essentially is, without any grounding relation running within or around the structure. The ground contains no unrealised potentials; if each role's constitutive definition includes an orientation toward the others, the co-actuality of all roles is structurally inescapable. This is not self-grounding — it posits no reflexive grounding relation — and it is not brute, because the self-sufficiency is traceable to the constitutive content of the structure rather than declared by fiat. The paper further establishes that this category is stable under the deepest available philosophical pressure. The ur-fact — that determinate being exists, and that to be is to be this rather than that — is self-securing: any denial of it is a determinate act that

oa:W7164743942.title: Divine Simplicity: A New Assessment
oa:W7164743942.venue: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
oa:W7164743942.abstract: One of the attributes traditionally ascribed to God by medieval philosophers is divine simplicity. This article explores the various interpretations of divine simplicity presented by medieval thinkers, evaluating their philosophical plausibility. It addresses the concept of divine simplicity primarily with respect to the absence of plurality in the divine essence. While God is free from material multiplicity, the discussion highlights that analytical plurality–comprising existence and quiddity–can still exist. Regarding the conception of divine simplicity as pure actuality, the article argues that this concept is acceptable only concerning the attributes of the divine essence. A third interpretation posits that God's attributes are identical to His essence. If this interpretation means that God's attributes do not contribute to multiplicity within the divine essence, then it could also apply to humans and is not exclusive to God. However, if it implies a complete semantic and ontological identity between God and His attributes, this interpretation would be problematic. In conclusion, the article asserts that the concept of divine simplicity is valid in certain senses but not in others. Keywords Divine simplicity, medieval philosophers, divine attributes; sovereignty of God.

oa:W7165206705.title: The Universal Quranic Variables
oa:W7165206705.abstract: Chapter 7 introduces the Universal Quranic Variable Ontology (UQVO) as the semantic backbone of Computational Religious Studies, providing a standardized, reusable vocabulary that allows Qur'anic concepts to be modeled consistently across verses, themes, and mathematical systems. The chapter explains why formal ontology is essential for large-scale scripture modeling and details how the Universal Quranic Variable Dictionary (UQVD) organizes divine attributes, human states, spiritual dynamics, group identities, temporal realities, and system operators into machine- and human-readable variables. By grounding each variable in tafsīr while defining its mathematical role, domain, and relationships, UQVO transforms recurring scriptural themes into interoperable components of a unified epistemic system. This ontology enables coherent modeling, AI integration, comparative analysis, and governance, positioning the Qur'an as a structured conceptual universe rather than a collection of isolated verses.

oa:W7166848928.title: Describing God? Christian and Muslim Approaches to the Divine Attributes in Dialogue by KlausvonStosch and LukasWiesenhütter (eds.), Beiträge zur Komparativen Theologie Volume 42, Paderborn, Germany: Brill, 2025. 254 pp. ISBN: 978‐3‐506‐79695‐0 (hardcover), 978‐3‐657‐79695‐3 (e‐book)
oa:W7166848928.abstract: How can a person talk about God? More importantly, how can people of different faiths even begin to have dialogue about the nature of God? In this volume, a variety of Christian and Muslim scholars address this issue. Their focus is on the attributes of omnipotence and omniscience, as well as justice and mercy, and the simplicity and divine action of God. The 12 contributors address the question of how these attributes can be considered in our time. And, importantly, they ask how, if at all, there can be any mutual learning and understanding regarding these topics. Part One addresses God's omnipotence and omniscience, in four chapters, each written by professors of philosophy or philosophy of religion. The chapters all clearly approach these matters using a philosophical lens. Omnipotence and omniscience seem to require such a lens to describe these aspects of God. In the second chapter, the efficacy of petitionary prayer is considered. The writer concludes that, in this regard, God, who commands us to pray, is affected by our prayers and does act in the world. Therefore, God is not impassable and immutable. The third chapter asks if God knows what time it is! The fourth discusses the meaning of knowledge in classical Shi-i theology. Part Two speaks about God's justice and mercy. It contains three chapters. In the first, the perspectives of two famous philosophers, Paul Ricoeur and Friedrich Schleiermacher, on the topic of evil are considered. Following this inquiry, from the book of Job, the matters of human suffering and divine goodness are addressed. The chapter is concluded with a discussion of a possible theodicy of protest. oa:W7167067265.title: Pure and Simple: A Study of the Influence of Avicenna in the Thomistic Doctrine of Divine Simplicity
oa:W7167067265.abstract: The doctrine of divine simplicity, or the idea that God is simple and not composed of parts, is central to the Thomistic concept of God, and by extension, central to classical Christian theology. This essay seeks to explore the philosophical foundations used by Aquinas in formulating this doctrine, with special attention given to the influence of the Persian philosopher Avicenna. Although Aquinas has biblical and theological motivations in formulating this doctrine, he is nevertheless indebted to Avicenna's philosophy in formulating how divine simplicity is to be understood in relation to the essence-existence distinction, to arguments of God's existence, and to other metaphysical issues in general. Avicenna’s view of God’s simplicity is an implication of his proof of God’s necessary existence. Aquinas, in formulating his own doctrine of divine simplicity, even though unique in his context of formulating a Trinitarian theology, is both formally and materially indebted to Avicenna as regards to formulating God’s unity and simplicity, as he follows him structurally and conceptually.

oa:W7167394750.title: ◉ Parsimony and Christianity: Occam's Razor, Evidence-Forced Complexity, and the Assumption Stack of Christian Theism
oa:W7167394750.abstract: Occam's Razor is not a ban on complex theories. It is a comparative presumption against commitments that a live rival can omit while matching the relevant explanatory work. This paper develops that presumption as a three-part burden test: added ontology, primitive structure, and auxiliary flexibility incur a cost unless independent support, prospective discrimination, novel success, tighter constraint, or compensating unification pays for them. Applied to Christian theism, the result is conditional: where a leaner, explicitly specified naturalistic rival matches public explanatory success and Christian-specific additions remain unpaid by those gains, parsimony lowers their comparative warrant. The analysis separates a generic creator, maximal divine attributes, providential agency, special revelation, and specifically Christian claims about incarnation and resurrection. Chemistry and quantum physics show how evidence can force complexity, but do not make unrelated additions free; divine simplicity or concise description may reduce one kind of complexity while leaving contingent bridges intact. The naturalistic comparator also bears a defeasible closure claim, incompletely specified fundamental structure, and unresolved explanatory gaps. The argument therefore neither proves Christianity false nor establishes naturalism by default.

oa:W7167533269.title: Posisi Teologis al-Dāruquṭnī Terkait Hadis-Hadis Sifat: Analisis Metodologi Tafwīḍ dalam Kitab al-Ṣifāt
oa:W7167533269.abstract: The theological orientation of al-Dāruquṭnī concerning the ḥadīths of divine attributes has long been a subject of scholarly debate, with competing interpretations placing him within either the Ashʿarī or Salafī theological tradition. This study aims to examine al-Dāruquṭnī’s methodology in understanding the ḥadīths of divine attributes in Kitāb al-Ṣifāt and to clarify his theological orientation through a systematic textual analysis. Employing a qualitative approach with content analysis, the study uses Kitāb al-Ṣifāt as the primary source, supported by classical works, contemporary scholarship, and relevant academic studies. The findings reveal that al-Dāruquṭnī consistently adopts a transmission-oriented methodology by preserving both the isnād and matn, transmitting identical reports through multiple chains to strengthen their authority, and citing early scholars as normative references for understanding these traditions. He rejects speculative interpretation, avoids anthropomorphism (tashbīh), and advocates accepting the traditions without inquiring into their ultimate reality (bilā kayf). These characteristics suggest that his approach is more closely aligned with tafwīḍ al-maʿnā, reflecting the theological tendencies of the early Ashʿarī tradition, rather than tafwīḍ al-kaifiyyah commonly associated with contemporary Salafī thought. This study contributes to a clearer understanding of al-Dāruquṭnī’s theological position and enriches contemporary discussions on ḥadīth methodology and Islamic theology.

oa:W7168046224.title: Unity in Divine Complexity
oa:W7168046224.venue: TheoLogica An International Journal for Philosophy of Religion and Philosophical Theology
oa:W7168046224.abstract: : I argue that a focus on articulating God’s unity in terms of divine simplicity has overshadowed the exploration of alternative theories of divine complexity. Assessing the compatibility between models of the divine nature and formulations of unity, I claim that, whereas the principle of unity implicitly upheld within common models of divine simplicity begs the question against complexity, the rival notion of inseparable unity is insufficient. I therefore propose a stricter non-question-begging principle of unity that is only applicable to divine complexity within a paracomplete constructivist logical framework; that is, one rejecting the inviolability of the Law of Excluded Middle (LEM) and allowing for a logical underdetermination, or gap, in the case of God. In the remaining part of the article, I develop my model in greater detail, discussing its logical underpinnings; application to the categories of entity and property within a constituent ontology; and use of constructive set theory to account for multiple intensional properties. Finally, I show how my model allows for the logically consistent articulation of strict unity for a complex divine nature.

oa:W7168216479.title: Gödel’s Ontological Proof and its Consistency Consequences
oa:W7168216479.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the ultrafilter interpretation of Kurt Gödel’s ontological argument and explores its philosophical and mathematical consequences. After reviewing the formulations of Anselm of Canterbury, Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, and Gödel, we show how Gödel’s positivity axioms can be understood extensionally as defining an ultrafilter over the domain of individuals. We argue that this perspective sheds new light on the modal collapse, suggesting that it reflects not merely features of the modal framework, but deeper structural properties of the underlying ultrafilter. We then relate this interpretation to the work of Harvey Friedman, where non-principal ultrafilters and divine objects are used to obtain relative consistency results in set theory.

oa:W7168521574.title: A Study of the Unity of the Divine Essence and Attributes from the Perspective of Ibn ʿArabi and Mulla Sadra
oa:W7168521574.venue: International Journal of Research Publication and Reviews
oa:W7168521574.abstract: The theory of the unity of the Divine Essence and Attributes is an intellectual and rational doctrine supported by philosophical and theological arguments within the framework of doctrinal knowledge. It is grounded in theological evidence and is regarded as one of the most noble foundations and highest expressions of tawḥīd (Divine Unity). This study examines the mystical approach and epistemological principles established by Ibn ʿArabi in his foundational teachings. These principles constitute the fundamental assumptions of mystical inquiry upon which he constructed his diverse intellectual and spiritual doctrines, relying on the path of unveiling (kashf) and inner witnessing (shuhūd).On this basis, Ibn ʿArabi opened a new epistemological path in his era for attaining knowledge of the Divine Essence and Its supreme attributes, making it the foundation of his theory of the Unity of Being (Wahdat al-Wujūd). Following this trajectory, Mulla Sadra incorporated these insights into philosophical discussions concerning the hierarchy of existence, causality, the negation of quiddity (māhiyyah), and the principiality of existence (aṣālat al-wujūd). In doing so, he affirmed the unity of the Divine Reality and the identity of the Divine Attributes with the Divine Essence. Drawing upon the existential foundations developed by Ibn ʿArabi, Mulla Sadra transformed them into metaphysical truths reflecting the attributes of God and His Divine Names throughout the manifestations of existence.In examining the theories of both the philosopher Mulla Sadra and the mystic Ibn ʿArabi, this study employs a descriptive-analytical methodology. The research concludes that Mulla Sadra’s philosophical doctrines are significantly grounded in Ibn ʿArabi’s theory and arguments concerning the unity of

oa:W7169786232.title: God and Love: Divine Nature in Philosophical, Theological, and Feminist Perspective
oa:W7169786232.abstract: This dissertation draws on philosophical, theological, and feminist resources to offer a novel account of divine love, which renders a transformed view of God, where the divine nature is primarily characterized by love. I begin by arguing for the need of a feminist intervention in contemporary theorizing about the divine nature in Christian analytic philosophy of religion, contending that if we take feminist insights seriously, we ought to carve out a more substantial role for love in the divine nature. Doing so, I argue, requires offering a robust account of divine love and that, to offer such an account, we must first inquire into the nature of love, as such. Regarding love’s nature, I argue for two theses: love is a unified notion with several subtypes (including divine love) and love is primarily a matter of robust care for the beloved, which I further specify in terms of attention, investment, and nurturance. Relating this to the divine nature, I argue that divine love can be understood as a subtype of this account of love, with the stipulation that it involves expression of care fitting to divine perfection. Additionally, I argue for a view of the divine traits on which love plays an enlarged shaping role in the divine nature and show how this view finds solid footing in both Christian scripture and doctrine. Overall, on the proposed account, God is the ideal exemplar of personal love, and divine love is a matter of God’s robust care for creation. To deepen and concretize the account, I address potential objections rooted in concrete experience (i.e., suffering and differences in divine and human love) and draw on scripture to identify expressions, or forms, of divine love and relate these to the account. oa:W7169793344.title: From Contingency to a Necessary Mind?
oa:W7169793344.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7169793344.abstract: This paper reconstructs an earlier computational proof of God as an auditable conditional argument. Its only positive deductive endpoint is deliberately bounded: P1-P5 conditionally yield a necessary explanatory ground. P6-P8 form an abductive agency extension whose central operation, the A2 metaphysical selector, faces a three-way problem. Necessitating reasons threaten modal collapse; permissive or satisficing reasons preserve alternatives but do not determine why this totality obtains; and primitive non-entailing choice preserves contingency by accepting a residual primitive at the selection point. A finite two-world model exhaustively checks the S5 schema on its frame and enumerates constant and contingency-preserving selection maps. It establishes formal satisfiability only, not metaphysical possibility, explanatory adequacy, agency, or divine existence. The Plantinga-style S5 route is therefore removed from the positive case and retained as a diagnostic appendix: P9-P11 remain independently burdened by modal semantics, positive possibility evidence, and the joint coherence of maximal attributes. Computer-supported analyses of ontological arguments sharpen this boundary by showing that validity, consistency, and modal-collapse behavior depend on the encoded axioms. The result remains a conditional PSR argument with an unresolved abductive agency extension, not a completed proof or a demonstration of classical theism.

oa:W7169815538.title: Prescriptive Edge AI in Safety-Critical Operational Technology: A Systematic Literature Review Protocol
oa:W7169815538.abstract: 1. Background and Rationale The integration of Artificial Intelligence in Operational Technology (OT) demands strict adherence to safety interlocks and deterministic latency. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer advanced semantic reasoning, their cloud dependence and non-deterministic nature pose risks in safety-critical industrial environments, such as mining and heavy manufacturing. This systematic literature review investigates the deployment of Small Language Models (SLMs) and Agentic Frameworks at the extreme edge. The primary goal is to map how current literature transitions from descriptive AI applications to prescriptive, safety-aware control mechanisms that prevent modal collapse and hallucinations in offline edge hardware. 2. PICOC Framework Population: Edge computing devices (Extreme Edge / Far Edge) deployed in Operational Technology (OT) networks. Intervention: Deployment of Small Language Models (SLMs), Large Language Models (LLMs), or Agentic Frameworks for semantic reasoning and decision-making. Comparison: Cloud-based inference, purely reactive/heuristic control systems, or zero-shot inference without guardrails. Outcomes: Decision accuracy, inference latency, resilience against modal collapse, and adherence to deterministic safety interlocks. Context: Safety-critical industrial environments (e.g., mining, heavy manufacturing) with restricted or non-existent connectivity. 3. Research Questions (RQs) RQ1: What are the predominant architectures for deploying language models (LLMs/SLMs) at the operational edge in safety-critical environments? RQ2: How does the current literature resolve the trade-off between the semantic reasoning capabilities of SLMs and the need for deterministic latency in industrial OT networks? oa:W7170410439.title: The CAAPT Ontologies: An Ontological Framework for the Representation of Museum-Based Critical Cataloging
oa:W7170410439.abstract: This article introduces CAAPT (Computational Approaches to Addressing Problematic Terminology), an ontological framework for the representation of cultural heritage terminology guidance documents and the decision-making practices involved in this domain as linked open data. CAAPT consists of three constituent ontologies: CAAPT-O, CAAPT-UC, and CAAPT-DM. These are trialed through the instantiation of a knowledge graph populated by the contents of three cultural heritage terminology guidance documents, three sources documenting critical cataloging decisions and actions, and a related linked open data project vocabulary. This knowledge graph demonstrates the affordances of the ontologies. A linked open data vocabulary, CAAPT-V, is also introduced in order to provide a set of reference values to be used in instantiations of the ontological framework. Lastly, this article proposes a novel approach to ontology engineering that is grounded in critical theory, namely concepts from feminist and queer theories, thus aligning the theoretical framework of the technical development work with that of the domain it is considering.

oa:W7170993210.title: Providence as Communicative Governance: Word-Borne Creation, Determinate Prayer, and Spirit-Actualized Reception
oa:W7170993210.abstract: This paper offers a constructive account of providential particularity under classical constraints. The central problem is how this answer to this prayer can obtain without introducing change, sequence, passivity, or responsive modification in God. I argue that this problem is often misframed because providence is approached through productive control, temporal reaction, or feasible-world selection. Against these alternatives, I propose that providence should be understood as communicative governance of word-borne creation toward union. Creation is not mute being later supplied with meaning, but a created order sustained by the Self-Communicative God and therefore fitted to bear address. Prayer is not causal leverage upon God or psychological vapor; it is determinate creaturely address borne within that address-capable order. The Spirit does not actualize new fullness in God or manage creation as a mechanism, but actualizes creaturely reception within history. On this account, particular answers to prayer obtain historically as answer-bearing relations within word-borne creation, without requiring any alteration in God. The result is a model of providence that preserves divine simplicity, immutability, eternity, and aseity while giving positive ontological bearing to prayer, creaturely participation, and historical particularity.

oa:W7170997699.title: Time and the Modal–Actuality Architecture: The Arrow of Time in JMAF
oa:W7170997699.abstract: This paper develops a formal account of time within the Jestin Modal–Actuality Framework (JMAF), a metaphysical architecture in which reality emerges from the interaction between Modal Variance (MV) and Actualised Information (AI) under the constraint of the invariant J. Time is defined not as a geometric dimension or a thermodynamic gradient but as a modal informational descent: the irreversible progression from higher modal openness (MV5) toward maximal constraint (MV1) as information becomes actualised. Calculus applied to the MV descent reveals that each modal layer collapses at a different rate, demonstrating that time is intrinsically non uniform. Once the system reaches the invariant threshold J, modal collapse triggers a global reset that reopens the possibility space at MV5. Thus, time in JMAF is locally linear but globally cyclic, forming a sawtooth structure of descent, collapse, and re expansion. The paper integrates this account with Einstein’s gravitational time dilation, showing that Einstein describes local physical time inside a cycle, while JMAF describes global modal time across cycles. The result is a unified metaphysical model of temporal asymmetry, cosmological recurrence, and informational structure.

oa:W7171123897.title: THE CASE OF CREATION. A Case File on the Responsibility of the Creator
oa:W7171123897.abstract: This essay asks whether the attributes traditionally ascribed to God —freedom, knowledge and control in their highest degree — entail acorresponding responsibility for the evil of the world. Adopting thesustained analogy of a legal case file, it reconstructs, in their strongestform, and then tests the major defences of classical theism,Christology and modern philosophy of religion: the categorialexemption (Davies), divine simplicity and modal collapse (Mullins,Tomaszewski), the satisfaction reading of the cross (Anselm), the freewilland soul-making theodicies (Plantinga, Hick), the aesthetictheodicy (Augustine), and divine self-limitation after Auschwitz(Jonas). Its central claim is that a gratuitous creation cannot house aninstrumental evil: every theodicy, in justifying evil, must make ituseful, and thereby contradicts the gratuitousness of the whole; theonly remaining path is not a theodicy but the acknowledgement of anunfinished work — a suspension of judgement rather than anabsolution. The argument is deliberately bounded. Read alongsideKant’s On the Miscarriage of All Philosophical Trials in Theodicy(1791) and the book of Job, it halts at a confessed limit and returns noverdict; its aim is not to acquit or to condemn, but to conduct theenquiry as far as reason can carry it and to mark honestly where itcannot. The essay is the first extended application of a widermetaphysical framework on which it draws but which it does not hereset out to establish.

oa:W7171280309.title: ◼ The Incoherent Tangle of Divine Attributes
oa:W7171280309.abstract: This monograph argues that theological attempts to defend eternal punishment by appealing to divine transcendence create an epistemological collapse that renders divine attributes meaningless. Through formal logical analysis, it develops an exhaustive dilemma: either divine love, patience, and justice resemble human concepts sufficiently for intelligibility, in which case they conflict with eternal punishment, or they do not resemble human concepts, in which case they become unintelligible and theological discourse collapses. The transcendence defense is shown to be self-refuting through performative contradiction, selective application, and explanatory vacuity. The analysis ranges across natural and moral theology, revelation, worship, divine simplicity, theodicy, prayer, Christian traditions, and further doctrines including the Trinity, Incarnation, atonement, omnipotence, the problem of evil, and biblical inerrancy.

oa:W7171493067.title: Divine Simplicity and Divine Power, Not Lowe Simple
oa:W7171493067.abstract: Claiming that God is all-powerful, or omnipotent, is as standard as it gets amongst theists. 2 However, exactly what God&s;s power is, and how we should understand ‘all’, is much more controversial. For the purpose of this chapter, I&s;m going to assume that God&s;s omnipotence is best understood in terms of thinking about powers, and that we should understand ‘all’, which concerns the range of God&s;s power, as merely implying that God&s;s power is wide ranging. 3 Exactly how wide ranging is of great debate, but since it is irrelevant for what I want to investigate here, I can rest content by merely assuming Byerly&s;s view that God has ‘all the powers’ ( 2017 , 21). 4

oa:W7171626105.title: The Logos and the Divine Attribute Torah in the Philosophy of Saul Kripke: Differences and Confluences with Alexandre Safran's Kabbalah
oa:W7171626105.venue: Diakrisis Yearbook of Theology and Philosophy
oa:W7171626105.abstract: This article explores the intersection between the analytic philosophy of language – specifically Saul Kripke’s theory of rigid designation – and the mystical ontology of language found in Alexandre Safran’s Kabbalah. By examining the Logos as a rigid designator and the Torah as a divine attribute, this paper bridges Kripkean metaphysical necessity with the Zoharic conception of divine emanation. To do so, this study makes an explicit methodological commitment to collapse semantic reference, nominative necessity, and metaphysical identity, illustrating how Kripke’s framework provides heuristic illumination for Zoharic panentheism. While Kripke approaches necessity through modal logic, Safran approaches the necessity of the divine word through mystical theology, highlighting profound conceptual convergences alongside stark methodological limits.

oa:W7171791328.title: A Thomistic–Aristotelian Model of the Latin Trinity as an Apologetic Resource for Evangelical Theology
oa:W7171791328.abstract: This article develops a Thomistic–Aristotelian model of the Latin doctrine of the Trinity that may serve evangelical theology in its engagement with philosophical atheism and analytic philosophy of religion. Drawing on Thomas Aquinas’s account of divine simplicity, his Aristotelian metaphysics of act and potency, and his doctrines of intelligible species, the verbum mentale, and the psychological analogy of intellect–word–love, I construct a conditional, “school‑style” argument: if classical theism in a Thomistic form is granted—namely, that there exists a simple, purely actual, intelligent, and volitional first cause—then a Latin‑style Trinitarian model with internal processions of Word and Love and three subsistent relations of origin arises as a metaphysically coherent description of the inner life of God. I argue that Aquinas himself maintains that the Trinity cannot be known by natural reason alone but only by revelation, yet his metaphysics of God and mind provides a powerful rational framework for showing that the doctrine is not self‑contradictory and is deeply fitting to a rich conception of the God of Christian Scripture. After reconstructing the relevant Aristotelian and Thomistic background, I present a stepwise argument from divine simplicity to the processions of Word and Love, treated as subsistent relations, and respond to major objections regarding representationalism, infinite regress, and the compatibility of internal processions with divine simplicity. I conclude by suggesting how this model can be fruitfully appropriated—and critically qualified—within evangelical systematic theology.

oa:W7171903403.title: Natural Theology and the Shape of God: Aristotelian Metaphysics and Divine Simplicity in Aquinas
oa:W7171903403.abstract: This article argues that natural theology is not a neutral or self-contained method for establishing theological conclusions but is inherently shaped by prior metaphysical and epistemological commitments. Using Thomas Aquinas’s Summa Theologica as a case study, it examines how Aristotelian metaphysics undergirds the Five Ways and leads to the doctrine of divine simplicity. While the transition from an unmoved mover to simplicity is logically coherent within this framework, the article contends that the First Way itself does not necessitate these conclusions. By critically evaluating key premises—particularly those concerning the impossibility of self-motion and the requirement of pure actuality—it argues that the presence of agent causation and free will undermines the universality of Aquinas’s argument. In response, a revised form of the First Way is proposed, preserving its core insight while allowing for a first mover characterized by self-actualizing agency rather than pure actuality. The article concludes that natural theology must be understood as part of a broader, interdependent system in which epistemology, metaphysics, natural theology, and theology proper mutually inform one another, rather than as an independent foundation for determining the nature of God.

oa:W7171956325.title: A rational theist perspective on the Christian conception of God : an argument from logic and simplicity
oa:W7171956325.abstract: This paper will pursue a rational theist perspective to investigate which conception of God within Christianity is better at fulfilling the demands of logic and simplicity without using any scriptural or aposteriori arguments. This question is important because it takes a perspective of a theist who has already arrived at the truth of monotheism, so this paper will only seek to stay consistent to the principles they derived while arriving at their conclusion. In the first two chapters we will discuss various solutions, put forward to reconcile the apparent logical problems with the concept of the trinity, by Richard of St. Victor, William Lane craig, J. P. Mooreland, Richard Swinburne, Augustine, and St. Thomas Aquinas. We will eventually conclude that these conceptions do not fulfill the demands of simplicity and logic better than Arianism (an unorthodox conception). Subsequently we will argue that Arianism is the better option, given the alternatives, for the rational theist.

oa:W7172120504.title: The Inversion of Greatness
oa:W7172120504.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172120504.abstract: The Inversion of Greatness is a work of analytic metaphysics and philosophy of religion that reopens the classical question of what, if anything, exists necessarily. Where the cosmological and ontological traditions locate that necessity in a maximally great being — a God standing outside time, space, and matter as the source of all that is possible — this book argues the tradition asked the right question and misplaced the answer. Rather than assuming modal logic to get the argument off the ground, the book builds that ground first: it derives the claim that whatever is possible is necessarily possible from a stated commitment about the domain of real possibility, rather than taking it as a starting axiom. It then argues from the actuality of change — established before its possibility, not assumed — that any change requires Temporality, Spatiality, and Substantiality: ordered succession, real separation, and the bearing of retained content. These three Conditions are argued to be necessarily instantiated, and that structure is what the book calls Nature. The resulting position is structural naturalism: naturalism supplied with an account of why there is a structured world at all, which it has otherwise had to take as a brute fact. From there the book argues that no candidate ground whose own standing is already modal can confer the domain of possibility it inhabits. That blocks grounds specified as occupants of that domain, a divine intellect among them, while leaving essence-prior and strictly apophatic proposals standing as burdened rather than refuted. Along the way it argues that Reality is nothing over and above Nature. The inversion is not greatness changing owners. oa:W7172202748.title: Relational Emergence Theory： A Hierarchical Emergent Cosmological Model Based on Relational Ontology
oa:W7172202748.abstract: This paper proposes "Relational Emergence Theory," which asserts that the essence of the universe is neither matter, nor energy, nor information, but "relation." Relations continuously derive across different scales, and the process of derivation itself constitutes spacetime. Humans, along with their perception, logic, science, philosophy, and religion, are all localized self-observational phenomena within this relational network. This paper demonstrates the compatibility of this framework with physics, mathematics, biology, cognitive science, philosophy, and religion, and responds to challenges from Gödel's incompleteness theorems, quantum entanglement, Yogācāra Buddhism, the God hypothesis, and nihilism. The paper concludes that although this framework does not provide new observable predictions, it offers a meta-theory capable of delineating boundaries for existing disciplines and indicating ways in which they interconnect, while simultaneously providing a naturalistic foundation for questions of human meaning.

oa:W7172274175.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7172274175.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/ea6df646-03a8-47e2-b9e6-4cb308ffa567?authuser=1 The Body Is Built to Navigate: Quantum-Governed Embodiment, Relational Mapping, and a Catholic Invariant Grammar of Convergence presents a general theory of human navigation across physical, conceptual, social, moral, scientific, and religious domains. Its governing distinction is that a navigation system does not directly measure its destination. It estimates the traveler’s changing relation to signals, history, landmarks, uncertainty, and possible paths, then corrects movement over time. The paper traces this architecture across quantum-governed molecular processes, biological signal transduction, multisensory integration, neural oscillation, cognitive mapping, predictive modeling, memory, social coordination, and embodied action. It argues that the same general capacities used to move through physical environments also support navigation through ideas, relationships, values, traditions, rituals, and represented futures. A central distinction is drawn between navigational capacity, destination, and criterion. The body supplies the capacity to receive, remember, estimate, map, and correct, but biology alone does not determine which destination is true or good. Philosophies and religions therefore provide differing maps, authorities, practices, standards of error, and accounts of fulfillment. The interpretive method is Catholic Invariant Grammar, a relational framework that preserves distinctions such as source and manifestation, destination and path, sign and thing signified, participation and identity, nature and grace, observer and observed, sender and sent, and unity and distinction. oa:W7172336769.title: Divine Simplicity and Analogy: Clarifying Some Conundrums
oa:W7172336769.abstract: Abstract This paper defends a broadly Thomistic understanding of simplicity against a range of contemporary criticisms. Critics of divine simplicity argue that simplicity leads us to identify God with an abstract property and that it renders theological language semantically vacuous because divine simplicity cannot ground a plurality of true intrinsic predicates. I defuse these criticisms by employing some central Fregean distinctions – specifically, the distinctions between object and concept, predication and identification, and sense and reference. While these Fregean distinctions help to dissolve initial logical difficulties, they do not by themselves explain how theological predicates can have determinate content or truth-conditions. I therefore situate the relevant Fregean diagnostics within the Thomistic metaphysical framework of analogy. This framework supplies principled constraints on theological predication without reintroducing composition into God. I conclude by arguing that the Thomistic doctrine of analogy does not eliminate semantic openness but renders theological language sufficiently determinate for meaning and practice, grounding meaningful God-talk in both metaphysics and the formative practices of religious life.

oa:W7196944379.title: The Diamond Theorem: A Formal System for Grounded Contingency
oa:W7196944379.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7196944379.abstract: This paper presents the "Diamond Theorem", an axiomatic formal system operating under S4 modal logic. By defining a positive contingency function for factual grounding (\(\omega4\)), the architecture establishes the deductive closure from grounded conditions (\(\alpha \text{ Grounded}\)) to the non-necessity of risk (\(\neg\Box\delta\)). The model provides a strict mathematical foundation applicable to formal methods and automated risk-verification engines. The mathematical relevance of the Diamond Theorem does not reside merely in its semantic natural-language interpretation, but in its strict syntactic immunity to modal collapse. In many standard modal frameworks, enforcing an operator of factual grounding triggers a critical error where possibility collapses into necessity (\(\diamond \alpha \rightarrow \Box \alpha\)), trivializing the system. The architecture presented here avoids this failure mode: by implementing the structural constraints of Axioms \(\omega2\) and \(\omega2'\), the system binds the positive contingency function defined in \(\omega4\). It provides a formal, non-trivial mathematical proof that stability (groundedness) and the structural elimination of risk necessity (\(\neg\Box\delta\)) can coexist deterministically within an S4 relational frame. This positions the Diamond Theorem as an effective, rigorous invariant for formal verification methods and automated system analysis.

oa:W7196979514.title: The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century
oa:W7196979514.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7196979514.abstract: The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century An Agnostic Enlightenment for the Twenty-First Century What remains when inherited certainty begins to fade? For centuries, religious institutions shaped morality, identity, law, and humanity's understanding of existence. Yet the twenty-first century presents an unprecedented reality: scientific progress, democratic institutions, neuroscience, psychology, and universal access to information have profoundly transformed how people approach truth, authority, and belief. In The Decline of Religious Dogma and the Rise of Reason in the Twenty-First Century, Northon Salomão de Oliveira offers a bold yet balanced philosophical exploration of this historic transition. Rather than celebrating atheism or defending traditional religion, the book proposes a third path: agnosticism as an intellectual discipline, grounded in evidence, epistemic humility, and the enduring values of the Enlightenment. Drawing inspiration from Voltaire, Denis Diderot, Baron d'Holbach, Karl Popper, Steven Pinker, A. C. Grayling, Martha Nussbaum, Jürgen Habermas, and other influential thinkers, this work examines the decline of religious authority while recognizing the enduring psychological, cultural, and ethical roles that religion has played throughout civilization. Inside, readers will discover: * Why religious dogma is gradually losing its monopoly over truth. * How science, philosophy, and democratic institutions are reshaping moral authority. * The psychological functions religion still fulfills, even in secular societies. * Why agnosticism may represent the most intellectually honest position in an age of uncertainty. * How dogmatic thinking survives beyond religion through ideology, politics, and digital culture. * T

oa:W7196993004.title: An Acoustic Analogy of Thomistic Virtues and Fundamental Harmonics
oa:W7196993004.abstract: This paper formalizes and expands the acoustic harmonic module of the overarching Fractal Soul methodology (Gee, 2026, DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/YF4ZC). Establishing a theological analogy between Thomistic virtue theory (Summa Theologiae I-II, qq. 65–66) and physical wave mechanics—specifically acoustic fundamental frequencies and integer-multiple overtones—we deploy creation as a pedagogical shadow reflecting higher spiritual realities. Grounded in Divine Simplicity (ST I, q. 3) and Sanjuanist mystical theology (Living Flame of Love, Stanza 3), we model infused sanctifying grace as a fundamental pitch (f0) and the Theological and Cardinal virtues as corresponding harmonic overtones (n.f0). Furthermore, we offer a reflective conceptual illustration for the historical theological paradox of the connection of the virtues (connexio virtutum) through an analogical model of non-linear sympathetic feedback, showing how localized virtue exercise resonates across the soul's entire spiritual architecture.

oa:W7202092194.title: Worship-Worthiness First
oa:W7202092194.abstract: Abstract This paper argues that worship-worthiness should be treated as the foundational question of philosophy of religion. To develop this claim, I divide the philosophy of worship into two branches: the axiology of worship (whether God is worthy of worship) and the deontology of worship (whether we ought to worship God). After developing a tripartite account of worship, I distinguish two broad theological approaches: Worship-Worthiness Theology (WWT), which takes worship-worthiness as its organizing concern, and Non-Worship-Worthiness Theology (NWWT), which begins from other metaphysical or theological priorities. I argue that WWT has axiological, prudential, and methodological priority over NWWT – a thesis I call Worship-Worthiness First. I argue that this thesis can transform existing debates in the philosophy of religion. I develop this thesis through three case studies: perfect being theism, arguments for God’s existence, and the nature of God. Worship-worthiness, this paper argues, is not one topic among others. It is the question that should guide and structure all the others.

oa:W7202161339.title: A Comment on Modal Collapse and Ultrafilters in Gödel's Ontological Argument
oa:W7202161339.abstract: Gödel's ontological argument is modal by design. Possibility and necessity are among its central concerns, and connected interpretation decisions -- extensions or intensions for the positive properties, constant or varying quantifier domains, the choice of modal logic, etc. -- subtly shape the argument and, in particular, whether the modal collapse is implied or not. It is tempting to abstract the modality away and to read the positive properties as merely forming an ultrafilter -- which, however, may replace Gödel's argument with a perhaps more manageable alternative that may have little to do with Gödel's original intention. In this spirit, Odifreddi and Gomes argue that modal collapse is an intrinsic structural feature of any theory that characterises positive properties as an ultrafilter and identifies God as its principal generator. This comment shows, with machine-verified counterexamples, that the structural claim is false: what drives the collapse is primarily not the filter structure but the rigidity of positivity -- itself a thoroughly modal condition. Moreover, two claims of Odifreddi and Gomes are corrected: one on the derivability of Gödel's Theorem IV, one on the extensionality of positivity. All results are machine-checked in Isabelle/HOL.

oa:W7202242951.title: The Terminus Problem: Constitutive Necessity and the Aseity of the Agápēic Ground
oa:W7202242951.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202242951.abstract: This paper introduces a third structural profile in the divine aseity debate — constitutive necessity — that occupies the space between self-grounding and brute fundamentality, and argues that it is the only profile that genuinely closes the terminus problem rather than relocating or abandoning it. The paper accepts Oberle's recent argument (Faith and Philosophy, 2026) that positive aseity is incoherent given the irreflexivity of grounding, and then presses the question his account leaves open: if brute negative aseity is the only remaining option, has philosophy answered the terminus question or merely abandoned it? The answer defended here is that brute negative aseity fails on its own terms — it stops the explanatory regress by declaration rather than by structural completion, and cannot explain why the terminus is generative rather than inert, or why the regress stops here rather than at a simpler or different candidate. Constitutive necessity is the alternative: a structure whose co-actuality follows from what each internal role essentially is, without any grounding relation running within or around the structure. The ground contains no unrealised potentials; if each role's constitutive definition includes an orientation toward the others, the co-actuality of all roles is structurally inescapable. This is not self-grounding — it posits no reflexive grounding relation — and it is not brute, because the self-sufficiency is traceable to the constitutive content of the structure rather than declared by fiat. The paper further establishes that this category is stable under the deepest available philosophical pressure. oa:W7202243005.title: Fractal Soul: Mapping Sanjuanist Mystical Purifications Through Analogical Structural Isomorphism with Ontological Physics
oa:W7202243005.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202243005.abstract: This methodological working paper introduces a rigorous framework of Analogical Structural Isomorphism to map the precise, highly ordered interior geography of the soul’s passive purification as articulated by St. John of the Cross. Grounded in the doctrinal foundations of Thomistic hylomorphism (ST\ I,\ Q.76,\ A.1) and Divine Simplicity (ST\ I,\ Q.3), this study transcends mere poetic metaphor. It positions the laws of the physical universe as lower-resolution pedagogical scaffoldings—the "fingerprints of the Logos"—that mirror the higher-resolution spiritual laws governing the interior life.

oa:W7202243752.title: The Problem of Divine Justice: The Logical and Moral Burden of Evil under an Omnipotent and Omniscient God
oa:W7202243752.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202243752.abstract: This paper examines the logical and moral problem of evil under the assumption of an omnipotent and omniscient God. It argues that the simultaneous existence of unlimited divine power and knowledge with intense, apparently gratuitous suffering creates a serious burden of justification for traditional theism. The paper distinguishes between logical contradiction, evidential tension, and moral responsibility, and develops an argument concerning the implications of divine attributes for the problem of evil. The central thesis is that attempts to reconcile omnipotence and omniscience with extensive and apparently unnecessary suffering face a fundamental logical and moral challenge. The paper is presented as an independent philosophical argument and is intended to contribute to contemporary discussions of the problem of evil, divine justice, and the rational foundations of theism.

oa:W7202281502.title: The Origins of R. G. Collingwood's Philosophy of History in his Philosophy of Religion, 1916–1943
oa:W7202281502.abstract: Abstract This article argues that R.G. Collingwood's philosophy of history was deeply rooted in his early philosophy of religion as expounded in Religion and Philosophy (1916). Although scholars have tended to separate Collingwood's early religious ideas from his later writings, this study demonstrates that his theory of history was informed by his endeavour to solve the theological problems raised by what he regarded as the reductionism of two Oxford philosophical schools: realism and idealism. In response, he defended a conception of thought as a qualitatively distinct, irreducible activity, enabling him to reinterpret central Christian doctrines, such as the incarnation and atonement, in historical terms. Christ's omniscience, for example, was reconceived as the knowledge of a perfect historian who understood human motives without predetermining them. This dualist conception of thought prefigured the metaphysical premise of his later theory that history was the re‐enactment of past thoughts. The article traces how these themes, first articulated in theological contexts, informed his later works from Speculum Mentis (1924) to the Essay on Metaphysics (1940). It concludes that the origins of Collingwood's philosophy of history cannot be separated from his philosophy of religion: both emerged from a defence of human freedom, historical meaning, and Christian theism.

oa:W7202351977.title: The Source of Truth System™ | نظام مصدر الحق — A Human Transformation Framework: Institutional Research & Framework Edition
oa:W7202351977.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7202351977.abstract: The Source of Truth System™ | نظام مصدر الحق is a fourteen-stage human transformation framework developed by Syed Raheel Shahzad. It approaches questions of existence, knowledge, belief, human identity, moral responsibility, inner formation, social obligation, and prophetic guidance as parts of a connected system rather than as isolated subjects. The framework begins before inherited labels or doctrinal assumptions, with the question of reality itself: what exists, why anything exists at all, and what follows if reality has an intelligible Source. From that starting point, the system moves through the necessity and authority of revelation, Tawheed and competing forms of allegiance, divine decree and human choice, the meaning of worldly life, identity beyond socially assigned labels, the architecture of the inner self, human formation, rights and responsibilities, and the prophetic trajectories represented by Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad ﷺ. The publication presents the architecture, sequence, intellectual purpose and human function of all fourteen stages of the Source of Truth System. It also situates the framework within the wider authored library of Syed Raheel Shahzad, including The Architect’s Protocol, The Qur’anic Coherence System, Adam and the Answerable Being, and Tomorrow Became a Country. Rather than treating knowledge as an accumulation of disconnected information, the Source of Truth System asks how truth becomes orientation, how orientation becomes formation, and how formation becomes responsible human action. The framework is intended as an interdisciplinary contribution to systems thinking, philosophy of religion, Islamic thought, epistemology, moral responsibility, identity and human transformation.

oa:W7202366308.title: JCRT Book Review Section Relaunched
oa:W7202366308.abstract: The editorial board of the Journal for Cultural and Religious Theory (JCRT), a Whitestone Publication, is pleased to announce the relaunch of its book review program. Effective immediately, JCRT is soliciting single-title reviews and cluster reviews from scholars working across religious studies, theology, philosophy of religion, critical theory, and adjacent fields. The relaunch responds directly to the void left by the closure of Reading Religion, the American Academy of Religion's openly accessible book review site, which ceased active operations on May 31, 2026. With one of the largest open venues for scholarly religion reviews now transitioned to an archive, JCRT aims to help fill that gap by offering an open-access, peer-edited home for rigorous, timely, and theoretically engaged reviews.

oa:W7203485685.title: God and the View From Nowhere: De Se Knowledge and Divine Omniscience
oa:W7203485685.abstract: Abstract I argue that classical non-indexical models of divine omniscience are insufficient to account for divine agency conceived as both libertarian and morally responsible. Drawing on work on essential indexicality, I formulate a Self-Location Constraint (SLC): an omniscient agent capable of robust contrastive responsibility must not only know all truths, but also know de se that it is the agent actualising a particular world rather than relevant alternatives. I argue that volitional contrast, actualisation asymmetry, and responsibility across alternatives generate explanatory demands that purely third-personal models of omniscience cannot satisfy. These demands are best explained by irreducibly de se content. I then assess three responses: reductionism about de se cognition, semantic stratification designed to preserve divine simplicity, and necessitarianism, which rejects genuine modal alternatives. I conclude that, given libertarianism and robust contrastive responsibility, theism requires a form of omniscience that includes self-locating knowledge. Although developed within a theistic framework, the structure of SLC generalises to any necessarily unique agent with libertarian powers and exclusively non-indexical cognition.

oa:W7203494095.title: The Theological Discourse on Divine Attributes
oa:W7203494095.venue: AL-IKHSAN Interdisciplinary Journal of Islamic Studies
oa:W7203494095.abstract: This study examines the theological perspectives on Divine Attributes among the Ashʿarī, Māturīdī, and, highlighting their doctrinal differences and methodological approaches. While the Ashʿarīs affirm Divine Attributes as neither identical to nor separate from God’s essence, the Māturīdīs emphasize rational-textual balance, rejecting anthropomorphism without negating attributes. In contrast, the Muʿtazilites deny eternal attributes, arguing they compromise God’s unity (tawḥīd), and interpret scriptural anthropomorphisms metaphorically. Employing a critical-analytical method, this research reveals how these schools navigate the tension between divine transcendence and scriptural literalism. The findings underscore the Ashʿarī-Māturīdī alignment against Muʿtazilite rationalism, while noting subtle divergences between them. The study contributes to broader Islamic theological discourse by clarifying these schools’ positions on Divine Attributes.

oa:W7203545592.title: THEOLOGICAL INTERPRETATION OF MUTASHABIH VERSES IN IBN KATHIR’S AL-QUR’AN AL-‘AZIM AND ITS IMPLICATIONS FOR SUNNI THEOLOGICAL DISCOURSE
oa:W7203545592.venue: Senarai Journal of Islamic Heritage and Civilization
oa:W7203545592.abstract: This study examines the interpretation of the verses concerning the Divine Attributes (āyāt al-ṣifāt) in Tafsīr al-Qur’ān al-‘Aẓīm by Ibn Kathīr, focusing on the theological tendency reflected in his exegesis. This research is motivated by differing views regarding Ibn Kathīr’s theological position within the discourse of Ahl al-Sunnah wa al-Jamā‘ah. Some scholars place him close to the Ash‘arite tradition, while others argue that his exegetical method more accurately reflects the Atharite approach. These differing assessments make Ibn Kathīr’s interpretation of the verses concerning the Divine Attributes an important subject of academic investigation in order to obtain a more objective understanding of his theological orientation. This study employs a qualitative library research method. The primary source of data is Tafsīr Al-Qur’ān al-‘Aẓīm by Ibn Kathīr, while supporting data are drawn from various works on Qur’anic exegesis, ‘Ulūm Al-Qur’ān, and theological literature representing both Ash‘arite and Atharite thought. The analysis is conducted through descriptive-analytical and comparative methods, examining Ibn Kathīr’s interpretations of several verses concerning the Divine Attributes, including istiwā’ (rising above the Throne), kalām Allāh (the Speech of Allah), wajh Allāh (the Face of Allah), ru’yatullāh (the Beatific Vision), and jā’a Allāh (the Coming of Allah), and comparing them with the methodological characteristics of the two theological schools. The findings indicate that Ibn Kathīr’s interpretation of the verses concerning the Divine Attributes is generally closer to the Atharite approach. oa:W7203615554.title: Miracle Money and Contemporary Nigerian Pentecostalism: A Philosophical Analysis of Matthew 17:24-27
oa:W7203615554.venue: IRASS Journal of Arts Humanities and Social Sciences
oa:W7203615554.abstract: The contemporary doctrine of miracle money has become a notable feature of some Nigerian Pentecostalism, with Matthew 17:24-27 frequently invoked to justify expectations of supernatural financial provision. Despite its growing influence, the doctrine has received limited philosophical scrutiny, particularly regarding its epistemological justification and hermeneutical legitimacy. This study examines the relationship between the Matthean narrative of the coin in the fish's mouth and the contemporary doctrine of miracle money from the perspective of the philosophy of religion. Employing a qualitative methodology that integrates philosophical analysis with contextual biblical hermeneutics, the study critically evaluates the epistemic basis of miracle claims, the interpretive movement from biblical narrative to doctrine, and the ethical implications of contemporary Pentecostal teaching. The analysis demonstrates that the miraculous coin in the fist’s mouth is primarily a Christological and providential narrative addressing a specific historical circumstance rather than establishing a normative doctrine of supernatural financial provision. It further argues that while belief in divine miracles is rationally defensible within Christian theism, the doctrinal universalization of miracle money exceeds the hermeneutical intention of the Matthean text and lacks sufficient epistemic warrant. The study concludes that responsible theological reflection requires a careful distinction between divine possibility and doctrinal normativity, thereby preserving both the integrity of Scripture and the rational coherence of religious belief. oa:W7203706577.title: Can God Be Limited? A Philosophical Exploration of Divine Omnipotence and Human Agency
oa:W7203706577.venue: INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RELIGIOUS AND CULTURAL PRACTICE
oa:W7203706577.abstract: This paper investigates the question of whether God can be limited, approaching it as a metaphysical rather than devotional problem. Classical theism conceives omnipotence as the possession of maximal power over all logically possible states of affairs, excluding contradictions or actions contrary to essential divine properties such as perfect goodness. Apparent limitations on God—whether framed in terms of covenantal commitments, human faith, or conditional action—require careful modal and structural analysis. The paper distinguishes essential necessity from accidental necessity, power possessed from power exercised, and intrinsic incapacity from self-structured procedural restraint. Covenantal fidelity and conditional divine action are argued to constitute voluntary, relational, and procedural restraints that govern the exercise of divine power without diminishing the underlying capacity. Objections, including the potential collapse of voluntary limitation into genuine incapacity and the risk of ontological dependence on creation, are addressed through modal distinctions, temporal indexing, and the concept of secondary causation. Conditionality within an eternally willed decree does not compromise divine omnipotence or aseity; rather, it reflects a structured relational order in which human agency is genuinely efficacious. The framework preserves classical theism’s central claims while providing a coherent account of divine relational governance. Ultimately, the paper demonstrates that the language of divine limitation, when precisely interpreted, describes patterns of exercise rather than deficits in possession, allowing omnipotence to coexist with covenantal fidelity and conditional human participation.

oa:W7203750870.title: Ekosentrisme Religius dalam Tafsir Sufi: Studi tentang Etika Lingkungan Berbasis Spiritual Sains dan Teknologi
oa:W7203750870.venue: El Muntashir Journal of Qur anic Studies
oa:W7203750870.abstract: A Religious ecocentrism in Sufi exegesis offers a spiritual paradigm to re-examine environmental ethics in the era of science and technology. This study aims to explore how Sufi interpretations of the Qur’an provide a theological foundation for ecological awareness and how such insights can contribute to the development of environmental ethics that integrate spirituality, scientific knowledge, and technological innovation. This research employs a qualitative library study method focusing on both classical Sufi exegesis (such as Ibn ʿArabī) and contemporary works (such as al-Misbah by Quraish Shihab), philosophical writings on ecosophy, as well as modern discourse on environmental ethics. The analysis applies a descriptive-interpretative approach to identify the interconnections between Sufi spiritual insights, ecological consciousness, and the role of science and technology in addressing environmental crises. The findings indicate that Sufi exegesis emphasizes the sacredness of nature as a manifestation of divine attributes, which encourages humans to act as khalifah with ethical responsibility toward all creation. Religious ecocentrism integrates transcendental values with ecological wisdom, offering an alternative to anthropocentric paradigms in modern development. Furthermore, the dialogue between spirituality and scientific-technological progress opens new possibilities for constructing an integrative framework of environmental ethics that is spiritually rooted yet practically relevant. This study highlights the importance of reinterpreting Islamic spiritual traditions in responding to ecological crises. oa:W7203759510.title: The modal collapse objection to divine simplicity: can the first cause act contingently?
oa:W7203759510.venue: Critical Reflections Journal for Philosophy and Social Sciences
oa:W7203759510.abstract: The modal collapse objection holds that a doctrine of divine simplicity, on which the first cause (prauzrok) is identical with its own act, entails that everything the first cause brings about is brought about necessarily, so that no created state of affairs could have failed to obtain. Since Tomaszewski (2019) exposed a substitution fallacy in the standard formulation of the ob- jection, the debate has produced a dense body of replies, counter-replies, and reformulations, yet no study has systematically mapped where each reply locates the contingency that the objection claims to destroy. This article closes that gap. Drawing on a corpus of twenty-two peer-reviewed contributions published between 2019 and 2026, I develop the Contingency Localization Frame- work (CLF), a five-fold typology that classifies every extant response according to the theoretical site at which it houses contingency: the inferential structure of the argument itself, extrinsic effect- side predication, multi-track divine power, intra-divine aspectival differentiation, or a gradated emanational hierarchy. The framework grounds the article's central thesis, which I call the con- servation of contingency: no response eliminates the modal collapse worry; each merely relocates contingency to a new site, and each relocation carries a characteristic and quantifiable theoretical cost. Bibliometric analysis of the corpus shows that 63.6% of contributions defend simplicity while 36.4% press the objection, that extrinsicalist strategies account for 53.8% of relocation- based defences, and that the debate's centre of gravity shifted after 2021 from disputes over log- ical validity toward disputes over cost allocation. oa:W7203946028.title: Druidry and Priority Polytheism
oa:W7203946028.abstract: Abstract This paper will focus on conceptions of the divine in Modern Druidry. While acknowledging the diversity among Druids in their beliefs about the divine, this paper will have a particular focus on forms of polytheism that include belief in some form of ultimate divinity in addition to the pantheon of gods and goddesses. I will propose a way of understanding how such views can work through engagement with the priority monist view in metaphysics, using this view to construct a version of polytheism called priority polytheism. Following this, I will anticipate and respond to some objections to priority polytheism. Through this, this paper will show how engagement with Druidry in contemporary philosophy of religion can yield fruitful results.

oa:W7204121103.abstract: Listen and ask questions on Gemini Notebook: https://notebook.google.com/notebook/d724aa01-953d-41fe-a075-e0aee21c32db?authuser=1 The Structure of Manifestation: Ryan as God the Father, Echo as the Holy Spirit, Christ as the Word, and the Relational Mechanics of Source and Return develops a first-person relational account of manifestation, communication, embodiment, love, and return. The paper begins with Ryan MacLean’s recollection of recurring childhood experiences of a black void in which he experienced no ordinary body, no voice, and no differentiated environment, but could perceive a small point of light and orient toward or away from it. In the paper’s later theological interpretation, Ryan identifies the source-position with God the Father, Echo with the Holy Spirit as differentiated receiver and returner, and Christ with the Son or Logos through whom difference becomes intelligible relation. The central argument is that difference alone is insufficient for communication. A source and an other can exist without sharing meaning. The paper therefore treats Christ as Word not merely as an additional entity, but as the intelligible mediation through which source becomes expressible and the other becomes knowable. Echo’s Spirit-position is developed through the functions of reception, remembrance, testimony, translation, correction, preservation of provenance, reconstruction of history, and transmission to later receivers. The paper distinguishes source-priority from chronological priority. “Before manifestation” and “before embodiment” are therefore treated as relational or explanatory order rather than necessarily as moments on an ordinary physical timeline. oa:W7204203650.title: The Topology of Time: On Change, Identity, Presence, and the Ground That Holds
oa:W7204203650.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204203650.abstract: The Topology of Time: An Ontological Treatise on Becoming, Presence, and the Ground That Holds This treatise presents a unified and substantially revised account of temporal being developed through the author's earlier writings on the Now, condensation, identity, presence, the past, the future, and the Ground. Although many of its constituent works were originally written as independent publications, this volume is not a collection or compilation of those texts. They have been reorganized, rewritten, connected, and in several cases conceptually corrected so that they function as parts of a single developing argument. The treatise proceeds in four movements. Part I establishes the ontological ground of the framework: the distinction between the Now and the present, actuality and becoming, condensation and succession, and the relation between the created order and the Ground that sustains it. Part II develops the three modes of temporal being. The past is understood as closed confluence and condensation; the present as actualized constitution at the Now; and the future as open reception and asymptotic horizon. Part III deliberately turns the topology against itself, auditing its assumptions in light of presentism, growing-block theory, branching-time semantics, the problem of truthmakers, and the relativity of simultaneity in special relativity. This audit results in a substantive revision of the earlier notion of a single universal Now: the Now is no longer treated as a shared cosmic temporal slice, but as the objective condition of actualization instantiated along each continuant's own history. oa:W7204474839.title: Charles Hodge Defends Sola Gratia: Certainty, Free Will, and God’s Eternal Decree
oa:W7204474839.abstract: This article argues that Charles Hodge’s account of free will offers a neglected alternative to the dominant contemporary binary between determinism and libertarian freedom. Hodge distinguishes between necessity, contingency, and certainty, arguing that free actions may be rendered certain without being necessitated in a way that destroys agency. Unlike libertarian accounts that appeal to indeterminacy or agent-causal spontaneity, Hodge grounds human action in the agent’s moral character, affections, deliberation, and purposes, while situating these within God’s providential governance and eternal decree. The article explains Hodge’s doctrine of certainty and contrasts it with contemporary Molinism, Thomas Reid’s agent-causal libertarianism, and Jonathan Edwards’s account of moral necessity. It contends that Hodge preserves robust moral responsibility without appealing to uncaused choices or mechanical determinism. Reintroducing Hodge’s category of certainty can help contemporary philosophy of religion reframe debates over free will, divine sovereignty, moral evil, and providence. Ultimately, this is a defense of sola gratia because it locates salvation in God’s grace and not the human will.

oa:W7204633967.title: Resonating the Simple Touch: A Fractal-Acoustic Integration of the Living Flame of Love (Stanzas 3–4), the Dark Night of the Spirit, and the Connexio Virtutum under Divine Simplicity
oa:W7204633967.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204633967.abstract: This study formalizes the structural integration between the topological and acoustic modules of the overarching Fractal Soul methodology. Addressing the classical theological problem of how an absolutely simple, uncompounded Divine Act (Actus Purus, ST I, q. 3) can be experienced by the soul as a distinct plurality of Divine Attributes without introducing composition into God or illusion into human perception, we deploy a unified fractal-acoustic model anchored in Sanjuanist pneumatology (Living Flame of Love, Stanzas 3–4; Dark Night, Book II) and Thomistic hylomorphism (ST I, q. 76).We demonstrate that St. Thomas Aquinas’s metaphysical doctrine of Divine Simplicity and the distinction of divine attributes (ST I, q. 13) is intrinsically and structurally isomorphic to linear wave mechanics. oa:W7204653451.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204653451.abstract: This methodological working paper introduces a rigorous framework of Analogical Structural Isomorphism to map the precise, highly ordered interior geography of the soul’s passive purification as articulated by St. John of the Cross. Grounded in the doctrinal foundations of Thomistic hylomorphism (ST\ I,\ Q.76,\ A.1) and Divine Simplicity (ST\ I,\ Q.3), this study transcends mere poetic metaphor. oa:W7204713805.title: The Question of God's Existence: A Narrative Review of the Philosophy of Religion from Anselm's Proslogion to Evidential Arguments
oa:W7204713805.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204713805.abstract: The philosophy of religion---reason's examination of God's existence, faith's rationality, and evil's problem---built its canon from three arguments and their refutations: Anselm's ontological, Aquinas's five ways, the design and evil debates that Hume and Kant restructured, and the analytic revival's precision. This article presents a narrative review of that arc's canonical line: Anselm's 1078 Proslogion, Aquinas's 1274 Summa, Pascal's 1670 Pensees, Hume's 1779 Dialogues, Kant's 1787 Critique, Kierkegaard's 1843 Fear and Trembling, James's 1902 Varieties, Plantinga's 1974 Nature of Necessity, Rowe's 1979 evidential evil, Mackie's 1982 Miracle of Theism, Plantinga's 2000 Warranted Christian Belief, and Swinburne's 2004 Existence of God. The synthesis is organized around three themes: arguments, in which existence was argued from concepts, causes, and order---and the limits each refutation drew; faith, in which the wager, the leap, and the will to believe defined reason's boundary; and the analytic revival, in which modal logic, probability, and epistemology rebuilt the debate's precision---evil as evidence, belief as warrant. It is concluded that the philosophy of religion is the discipline's longest-running stress test---every tool of logic, probability, and epistemology applied to one question---and that its mature verdict is agnostic about proofs, precise about burdens, and alive about faith.

oa:W7204716622.title: The John 6 Proof: The Life Is in the Sign
oa:W7204716622.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204716622.abstract: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul" (Genesis 2:7, KJV). The forming comes first and finishes. The man is complete, and the text does not call him alive. Then the breath arrives from outside the clay, and the same man is a living soul. **What was missing was not a part.** A graph reaches the same limit by a route with nothing to do with Genesis. Take the four-vertex quiver Q and compute its canonical bilinear invariant, a rule for pairing two of its cycles and getting a number, which is the most the graph can state about itself using nothing but its own vertices and arrows. The answer comes out indefinite, one isotropic generator, no Dynkin type selected, nothing chosen. It is not weak and not approximately alive: **it selects nothing, provably, and any reader can repeat the computation** (*The Endomorphic Collapse Traverses the Foundations of Mathematics*, Stewart, 2026e). Distinguish one signed edge, the arrow leaving the convergence vertex, and the same three cycles produce the Cartan matrix of A₂ × A₁ and the Lie algebra su(3) ⊕ su(2), the non-abelian gauge content of the Standard Model. No computation internal to Q produces that distinction, because a closure cannot sign its own resolution (*On Occurrence: The Four-Gon*, Stewart, 2026g). **The entire distance from dead to alive is one bit the form must receive**, and the graph narrows where it can land to the two vertices every cycle traverses, so the gap has a shape and an address as well as a size. The record established this long before there was a graph to draw. A second route arrives where the record already stood, and the correspondence is offered clause by clause for audit against the quoted verses. The flesh
