oa:W7204805704.title: The Third Link: Why a Triadic Essence Admits Exactly Two Processions
oa:W7204805704.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7204805704.abstract: A long-standing objection to the triadic invariant's theological implications holds that the numerical coincidence between three factors (Pattern, Intent, Presence) and three divine Persons is derivationally inert — the Person-count comes from Aristotle's two-faculty psychology imported from outside, not from the factor structure itself. This paper closes the objection using two published results: the bisimulation proof of irreducibility (Shell, Wish, and Noise) and the structural filter eliminating every competing ontological ground via the Zero Test (The Self-Consuming Objection). The closure runs on the operational/ground asymmetry built into the factor definitions: Pattern and Intent are operational (they generate immanent acts when a simple essence reflects on itself), while Presence is the ground of actuality (it does not generate a procession — it IS the field in which processions occur). The warrant chain is made explicit: the physics program validates the definitions as structurally asymmetric; the definitions analytically entail the role-split; the split constrains the count. Divine simplicity is derived from the self-grounding requirement, not imported from classical theism. Two operational factors yield two processions; one ground factor yields one unoriginate source; 2 + 1 = 3 Persons.

oa:W7204924268.title: Ockham ante una cuestión espinosa: ¿cómo conciliar la omnisciencia divina con la contingencia del futuro?
oa:W7204924268.abstract: This paper deals with the controversy of the compatibility between divine omniscience and the contingency of future, concrete states of affairs. It attempts to make a formal reconstruction of William of Ockham’s solution in his Tractatus de praedestinatione et de praescientia Dei respectu futurorum contingentium. There is an alleged inconsistency between the following theses: (1) bivalence of future-tensed propositions (∀p ∈ Φ, ∀t ∈ T, ∀x ∈ ℕ: π (t, F(x) p) ∈ {0,1}); (2) necessity of the past (P(y)F(x)p ⊃ NP(y)F(x)p); and (3) divine infallibility (F(x)p ≡ DF(x)p). From these, a presumed modal collapse would follow: if at ta God knew that p would occur at tb (DF(x)p at ta), and if past truths are now necessary (NP(y)F(x)p), then it would follow that NF(x)p and therefore Np. Briefly, the precise assignment of a truth value would imply the necessity of the state of affairs denoted. Ockham, however, would show that this inference rests on false premises and there is no contradiction between maintaining God’s foreknowledge of the future, on the one hand, and the contingency of future concrete states of affairs, on the other. We will study his interpretation and formulation of the problem on the basis of his analysis of Chapter 9 of Aristotle’s Περὶ Ἑρμηνείας, and his formulation of the Aristotelian deterministic argument, which assumes a modal collapse between truth and necessity and implies that the Stagirite –according to Ockham’s reading– suspends the universal operativity of bivalence. Finally, we will show that the Ockhamist thesis represents an ordered and non-contradictory set of propositions and succeeds in generating a philosophically valid solution if interpreted within an appropriate formal framework of temporal logic. oa:W7205175174.title: İbn Sînâ’da İlahî Faillik, İrade ve Hürriyet
oa:W7205175174.abstract: One of the main criticisms directed at Avicenna’s conception of God in the history of Islamic thought is the claim that he conceived of God as an essentially necessitating cause (mūjib bi-l-dhāt) and thereby eliminated divine will and freedom. This criticism, systematized especially by al-Ghazālī in Tahāfut al-Falāsifa, later became a widespread assumption in kalām and philosophical literature, according to which the Peripatetic philosophers viewed God as a necessary, will-less, and natural cause. This article argues that this assumption should be reconsidered within Avicenna’s own metaphysical system. Its central claim is that Avicenna does not understand divine will as an independent faculty of choice added to God’s essence, but grounds it as an actual perfection to be interpreted together with knowledge, providence, approval, generosity, and wisdom. Based on textual and conceptual analysis, the study first shows the conceptual limits of the binary opposition between the freely choosing agent and the essentially necessitating cause, and then examines the divine attributes within the doctrine of the Necessary Existent. It further argues that emanation should not be read as a natural or mechanical compulsion, but as the necessary perfection of divine knowledge and wisdom. The tension between the kalām theory of choice and the Peripatetic doctrine of necessity is therefore interpreted not as a simple opposition, but as the result of different ontological assumptions about the nature and operation of will. Although al-Ghazālī’s criticisms are strong in terms of their kalām premises, they do not fully capture Avicenna’s specific understanding of will, knowledge, and necessity. oa:W7207625614.title: Fate in Ancient Greek Philosophy and Religion
oa:W7207625614.abstract: The Greek term heimarmene, rendered in Latin as fatum and in English as “fate” (and occasionally as “destiny”), designates a doctrinal notion situated at the intersection of Greek religion and philosophy. The analysis of the interplay between the purported causality of fate and that of other forms of causation is a complex undertaking, closely connected with a range of religious questions. Reflection on fate gives rise to fundamental philosophical issues, including those concerning contingent futures, freedom of the will, determinism, divine foreknowledge, and providence. Furthermore, this theme is intertwined with numerous human situations prominently depicted in Greek epic and tragic literature—indeed, it has exercised a lasting influence on Western literature as a whole. Such situations include unexpected good fortune, the mortal inability to withstand misfortune, the practice of divination, and the relationship between human beings and the divine. Given the enduring relevance of themes such as free will, determinism, and divine foreknowledge within contemporary philosophy of religion, it is particularly fruitful to investigate how these questions were addressed not only by Greek philosophers but also by other Greek authors who are not typically classified as philosophers. In late antiquity, Greek thought revisited the problem of fate and divine providence within the framework of Christian theology, engaging in close dialogue with so-called “pagan” philosophical traditions. These exchanges constitute a significant contribution to the metaphysical understanding of fate.

oa:W7208309334.title: The Reexamination of Spinoza's Philosophy of Mind (1)
oa:W7208309334.abstract: Today some scholors seem to have a tendency to see in Spinoza a precursor of Mind-Body Identity Theory or Double Aspect Theory, but the author stresses that one could interpret Spinoza's Philosophy of Mind the most consistently only if one approached it with the sufficient understanding of the quite peculiar terminology and logic of his metaphysical thought. In this paper the author tries to make clear those elements of Spinoza's metaphysics which could be decisively relevant to the exact and consistent interpretation of his Philosophy of Mind: first, the peculiarity of his concept of God as the unique Substance; second, the asymmetry between Thought and the other Divine Attributes; and third, the Principle of Intelligibility implied by his concept of Infinite Intellect.

oa:W7208753864.title: Between ʿIbādah and Muʿāmalah
oa:W7208753864.abstract: The Indonesian controversy over Salam Lintas Agama (SLA), intensified by the 2024 Ijtima` Ulama fatwa declaring Muslim participation in multi-religious greeting formulae impermissible, is commonly read either as a sociological problem of tolerance or as a settled doctrinal question. Existing scholarship has not adequately examined SLA as a contemporary masʾalah fiqhiyyah ijtihādiyyah whose legal evaluation depends on its takyīf (juristic characterization), whether positioned as `ibādah, mu`āmalah, or taḥiyyah ijtimā`iyyah, and on the uṣūlī methods used across competing schools. This article addresses that gap. Employing a qualitative study of the SLA controversy as a national discourse, this research draws on in-depth interviews with key informants purposively sampled across several Indonesian locations (Jakarta, Bandung, Tana Toraja, and Papua) to capture maximum variation in actor positions, triangulated with classical fiqh literature, the 2019 MUI Jawa Timur taushiyah, and the 2024 fatwa. Three complementary lenses structure the analysis: Social Identity Theory maps boundary-work activated by SLA; Hayden’s antagonistic tolerance characterizes its public-space dynamics; and Maqāṣid al-Sunnah reading of the prophetic ḥadīth on greeting provides the normative interpretive frame. Findings show that SLA is classified as `ibādah when foregrounded as a doctrinal speech-act invoking divine attributes, and as mu`āmalah/taḥiyyah ijtimā`iyyah when foregrounded as civic recognition; the shift is governed by niyyah, `urf, maṣlaḥah, and sadd al-żarāʾi`. The article contributes to comparative madhhab scholarship by demonstrating that the SLA dispute is fundamentally a methodological disagreement among fiqh schools. oa:W7209313276.title: 9781003202172_10.4324_9781003202172-8.pdf
oa:W7209313276.abstract: Defenders and critics of divine simplicity rightly look to Thomas Aquinas’s important contributions to this pillar of classical theism (=CT). But few contemporary discussions notice the way Aquinas employs pseudo-Dionysius’s triplex via as a principled heuristic that governs and organizes his theological enquiries concerning divine simplicity. This oversight has led to misinterpretations of Aquinas’s doctrine of divine simplicity (=DDS), which must be situated within his triplex via theology (=TVT). In this chapter I show that, like Aquinas’s DDS, the value of Thomist TVT extends beyond historical exegesis and provides exponents of CT with a fertile alternative to the more well-known Anselmian inspired heuristic of perfect being theology (=PBT). In the first part I introduce two problems for CT that cannot be resolved by PBT and Thomistic accounts of DDS that omit Aquinas’s TVT. In the second part, I explain what Thomistic TVT is and why its integrated threefold way of understanding God via causality, negation, and super-eminence can overcome these problems for CT.

oa:W7211921329.title: Cosmological Emergent Materialism
oa:W7211921329.abstract: Theism holds that the uncreated ground of existence is a someone. This paper argues it is a something. The disagreement is isolated to a single premise. That something is uncaused is common ground, and the divergence is over what kind of thing it is. Two routes are given to that conclusion. One runs from the organisation-dependence of consciousness, supported by the cortex-cerebellum dissociation, the clinical validation of an organisation-based index, and an anaesthetic dissociation of consciousness from behaviour. The other runs from the observation that selection requires differentiation, which turns divine simplicity from an escape into a dilemma with modal collapse on its other branch. Three further claims are defended. Fine-tuning is a defect indicator in physics rather than a design indicator. The constants show no optimisation signature, which an unselected ground predicts and a selecting one does not, and which is a published result rather than an impression. Experience is bounded in cosmic time by the thermodynamics of dissipative structure. Nine objections are addressed, including Strawson's argument that physicalism entails panpsychism, Saad's psychophysical harmony argument, and Cutter and Saad's problem of nomological harmony. Three of them are shown to construct a coordination problem by first splitting one thing into two. The paper claims viability and an accurate account of its own costs, not a refutation of theism, and it states what would show it wrong.

oa:W7211995787.title: The Necessity of Unity and the Contingency of Distinction
oa:W7211995787.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7211995787.abstract: This paper develops the philosophical implications of Permanent Unity: Probability, Closure, and the Mathematics of Changing Distinction. It asks whether a whole may remain necessarily reconciled to unity while its internal distinctions remain genuinely variable or contingent. Starting from the invariant-closure architecture of Permanent Unity, the paper introduces a restricted modal interpretation in which unity holds across every admissible articulation while particular distinctions need not. This yields a Structural Modal Separation result: necessary closure does not entail necessary articulation. The mathematics is elementary; the contribution lies in identifying and developing its modal and ontological significance. The argument is situated within the long history of the problem of unity and multiplicity, including Parmenides, Plotinus, Anselm, Spinoza, Whitehead, contemporary work on probability invariance, and debates concerning necessity, contingency, divine simplicity, and modal collapse. It also considers the importance of unity across several major philosophical and religious traditions without treating those traditions as equivalent or deriving any theological conclusion from the mathematics. The resulting proposal is deliberately bounded. Structural necessity within a declared mathematical architecture is not automatically metaphysical necessity. Nevertheless, the mathematics establishes the formal compatibility of invariant unity with changing distinction and motivates a broader ontological question: whether plurality divides reality, or instead constitutes internal articulation of a unity that is never abandoned. oa:W7212118994.title: Does Aristotle’s Theory of Relativity Commit Him to Protagoreanism?
oa:W7212118994.abstract: Perceptual Modal Collapse is the view that no unperceived perceptibles exist. Aristotle takes Perceptual Modal Collapse to be central to Protagoreanism. But Aristotle’s Categories 7 commits Aristotle to Perceptual Modal Collapse: perception and perceptible correlate; each relative pair is constituted by its relation to its correlative; correlatives exist at all the same times; so, perception and perceptible exist at all the same times. Hence, there are no unperceived perceptibles. Moreover, correlatives are simultaneous by nature. Aristotle’s arguments that this does not apply to perception and perceptible are unconvincing. I argue that Aristotle’s second definition of relatives can save Aristotle’s theory from Perceptual Modal Collapse, since the definition distinguishes perceptible as a schematic relative from specific perceptible qualities. Once we disambiguate, we can see that specific perceptibles need not exist at the same time as perceptions. Thus, the specific heat of a fire in a forest can exist, even when unperceived. These ideas underlie Aristotle’s account of intentional relatives in Metaphysics 5.15, where specific perceptual qualities are the content of perceptions.

oa:W7212135739.title: Kontinuitas Apokaliptik: Kajian Intertekstual Figur Anak Manusia dalam Daniel 7:13-14 dan Kitab Wahyu
oa:W7212135739.abstract: Debate concerning the identity of the mysterious figure of the ‘Son of Man’ in Daniel 7:13–14. The methodology employed is qualitative, utilising a literature review approach combined with Richard B. Hays’s intertextual analysis to trace the ‘echoes’ of the text of Daniel within the narrative of Revelation. But how does the Book of Revelation, through an intertextual approach, identify Jesus Christ as the figure of the “Son of Man” in Daniel 7:13–14 and affirm his Christological continuity and transformation within an eschatological context? Book of Revelation systematically identifies the glorified Jesus Christ with the figure of the “Son of Man”. This continuity is clearly evident through the use of similar terminology in Revelation 1:13 and 14:14, as well as the attribution of the divine attributes of the Ancient of Days to Christ. The study concludes that John undertook a Christological transformation that positions Christ as the definitive fulfilment of Daniel’s prophecy, holding universal authority and eschatological victory over the forces of evil. oa:W7212186029.title: Divine simplicity as symmetric parthood
oa:W7212186029.abstract: Abstract Taken at face value, the doctrine of divine simplicity (DDS) says that God lacks proper parts, but the doctrine is also often formulated as a thesis identifying God with all his parts. The two formulations are not generally equivalent – on some plausible mereological theories, something can lack proper parts by being a part of all its (possibly distinct) parts. Thus, the DDS can be alternatively formulated as a thesis saying that God is part of all his parts – call this the symmetry formulation. The symmetry formulation is viable as a thesis about God’s relation to his attributes, because instantiation can plausibly be modelled as parthood. Moreover, the symmetry formulation retains the usual motivations for divine simplicity coming from the doctrines of aseity, transcendence, immutability, and unity. The symmetry formulation also addresses common objections to divine simplicity regarding distinctness in God’s attributes and those coming from modal collapse arguments.

oa:W7212411213.title: No World to Return To: The Modal Collapse of Radoilska's Fixed-Capacity Account of Agency
oa:W7212411213.abstract: The Kantian division between theoretical rationality and practical reason is not a settled feature of the philosophical landscape; it is the fault line along which rationalist theories of agency necessarily collapse. Lubomira Radoilska's Aristotelian programme, which grounds agency, autonomy, and moral responsibility in a fixed intrinsic capacity for rational self-governance and advances this capacity as the bridge between cognitive and practical norms, is the most sustained recent attempt to close that divide from within the rationalist tradition. This paper argues that the attempt fails by structural necessity. Any theory that posits a fixed capacity for rational self-governance as the ground of normative assessment generates four fatal contradictions: a normative contradiction across agents in different modal situations; the structural impossibility of individuating agential capacities; the unprincipled collapse of the boundary between pathological and merely difficult conditions of agency; and the impossibility of tracking the progressive temporal contraction of the accessible world-set through addiction and cumulative circumstantial disadvantage. The modal account of persons, in which a person at a given time is constituted by the set of worlds accessible under a person-specific accessibility relation grounded in her causal-psychological constitution, phenomenological horizon, and relational situation, is not one alternative among others. It is the only framework adequate to these phenomena, and it dissolves rather than bridges the Kantian divide by showing that theoretical and practical engagement with the world are two orientations toward the same modal structure of what is actually accessible from the agent's actual situation.

oa:W7212440680.title: After Clarity Comes Return: A Pilot Method for Mapping Tawbah, Inabah, Moral Repair, and Accountability in Qur'anic Discourse
oa:W7212440680.abstract: This paper develops and tests a pilot method for mapping the burden of clarity in Qur'anic argument. The study begins from a methodological problem in Qur'anic studies and philosophy of religion: the Qur'an repeatedly presents guidance as clarification, proof, sign, reminder, and argument, yet discussions of proof often move too quickly from isolated verses to apologetic conclusion, doctrinal assertion, or devotional reflection. What remains underdeveloped is a disciplined way to ask how clarity becomes morally binding inside the discourse itself. When does a text portray a listener as merely uninformed, and when does it portray that listener as already addressed, shown, warned, reminded, and therefore answerable? The paper proposes a structured coding model for bayyinah, hujjah, burhan, ayah, bayan, and related evidential terms as they function in Qur'anic argument. The model does not treat these terms as interchangeable synonyms. It distinguishes manifest clarity, demonstrative proof, binding argument, sign-based indication, explanatory disclosure, warning, response demand, and excuse closure. The pilot method records the type of clarity being presented, the addressee being addressed, the resistance being exposed, the response demanded, the threshold of accountability, and the evidential strength of the claim. Selected passage clusters are used to test whether this method can map the Qur'an's movement from communication to responsibility without reducing revelation to a mechanical argument chart or turning moral accountability into an unsupported judgment about actual persons. oa:W7212445153.title: Divine Revelation or Human Origin? An Epistemological, Historical, and Bayesian Analysis of the Qur'an (2nd ed.).
oa:W7212445153.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7212445153.abstract: Divine Revelation or Human Origin? is a critical study of the Qur’an’s origins through the lens of Bayesian reasoning, historical analysis, and inference to the best explanation. Rather than beginning from either faith or skepticism, the book asks a narrower question: given the evidence available to us, what can actually be established about whether the Qur’an is best explained by genuine divine revelation or by ordinary human and historical processes? The investigation compares competing revelation and human-origin models across a wide range of evidence, including the Qur’an’s Late Antique context, religious geography and diversity, cognition and religious belief, Adam and human evolution, the Flood, alleged textual and legal difficulties, literary inimitability, prophecy, miracle traditions, scientific-miracle claims, textual preservation, Egyptian historical knowledge, and the transmission of hadith. Throughout, the book distinguishes possibility from probability, compatibility from confirmation, undercutting from counterevidence, and local evidential judgments from global conclusions. It also examines how source uncertainty, dependence between arguments, retrospective selection, model flexibility, and differing theological commitments affect the strength of common apologetic and skeptical arguments. The result is deliberately restrained. The analysis finds that some popular arguments for revelation are substantially weaker than often claimed, while several skeptical objections also fail to establish what they are sometimes taken to prove. A number of arguments retain genuine conditional evidential force in either direction, but the study does not establish a defensible overall Bayesian ranking between divine revelation and human origin. oa:W7212551692.title: Деизм как теистическая гипотеза: кумулятивный абдуктивный аргумент
oa:W7212551692.venue: Вестник Удмуртского университета. Серия «Философия. Психология. Педагогика»
oa:W7212551692.abstract: В аналитической философии религии сохраняется открытая дискуссия о том, какая теистическая гипотеза является концептуально наименее проблематичной. В работе конструируется серийно-кумулятивный абдуктивный аргумент в пользу деизма по четырём взаимосвязанным линиям и выявляется структурное напряжение в классическом теизме с явным рассмотрением молинистских ответов. Исследование опирается на лейбницианское различение принципа достаточного основания в его версиях несесситации и склонения; на объяснительный разрыв в философии сознания; на эпистемологическую проблему Бенацеррафа в онтологии математики; на концептуальный анализ совместимости либертарианской теодицеи с систематическим Провидением. Показано, что деизм является рационально защитимой абдуктивной гипотезой. Концептуальное преимущество над классическим теизмом по критерию внутренней последовательности устанавливается при учёте молинистских ответов. Частичные структурные преимущества над рядом натуралистических позиций принимаются при условии принятия ненатуралистической онтологии. Эксплицитно зафиксированы шесть нерешённых структурных проблем: (i) невозможность непосредственной выводимости существования необходимого бытия из концептуального анализа необходимости, (ii) проблема деривации, (iii) проблема природного зла, (iv) проблема божественного выбора, (v) проблема доступности, (vi) проблема онтологии каузального акта. The question of which theistic hypothesis is least conceptually problematic remains open in analytic philosophy of religion. This paper constructs a serial-cumulative abductive argument for deism along four interconnected lines and examines the structural tension in classical theism with explicit consideration of Molinist responses. oa:W7213272302.title: জঞনতততব ও ধরমতততবর আলক সতয : একট তলনমলক আলচন (The Concept of Truth in Epistemology and Theology: A Comparative Discussion)
oa:W7213272302.abstract: The concept of truth is one of the central themes in both philosophy and theology. Epistemology and theology have advanced in the pursuit of truth with different methods and distinct objectives. Consequently, their presentations of truth also different. This paper attempts to analyze the nature and purpose of truth in the light of epistemology and theology. It discusses the methods and sources employed by philosophy and religion in justifying truth. On this discussion, the paper identifies possible areas of conflict between the two conceptions and proposes constructive solutions for resolving them. The aim of this paper is to demonstrate, through comparative analysis, that although epistemological and theological truths are distinct, they can complement each other and can play a vital role in flourishing human life.

oa:W7213352846.title: Resonating the Simple Touch: A Fractal-Acoustic Integration of the Living Flame of Love (Stanzas 3–4), the Dark Night of the Spirit, and the Connexio Virtutum under Divine Simplicity
oa:W7213352846.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213352846.abstract: This study formalizes the structural integration between the topological and acoustic modules of the overarching Fractal Soul methodology. Addressing the classical theological problem of how an absolutely simple, uncompounded Divine Act (Actus Purus, ST I, q. 3) can be experienced by the soul as a distinct plurality of Divine Attributes without introducing composition into God or illusion into human perception, we deploy a unified fractal-acoustic model anchored in Sanjuanist pneumatology (Living Flame of Love, Stanzas 3–4; Dark Night, Book II) and Thomistic hylomorphism (ST I, q. 76).We demonstrate that St. Thomas Aquinas’s metaphysical doctrine of Divine Simplicity and the distinction of divine attributes (ST I, q. 13) is intrinsically and structurally isomorphic to linear wave mechanics. The "deep caverns of feeling" (LFL 3) represent a recursive, nested fractal geometry (V \to 0, A \to \infty) shaped through active purgation (Ascent II–III) and dynamically tuned through the Passive Night of the Spirit (DN II). When the singular, uncompounded "breathing of the Holy Spirit" (LFL 4)—modeled acoustically as a simple fundamental driving frequency (f_0)—touches the soul, the pure wave does not alter or decompose. Instead, the distinct nested scales of the purified caverns respond through modal resonance, each cavern exciting its own native harmonic overtone (n. f_0) within the soul's created boundary conditions.These scale-dependent overtones correspond to the distinct "Lamps of Fire" (LFL 3; Divine Attributes) and mirror the proportional resonance of the connexio virtutum (ST I-II, qq. 65–66) held together in the single virtue garland of Sanctifying Grace (Spiritual Canticle, Stanzas 30–31). oa:W7213503803.title: ASEITY AND THE SUBSTRATE: What the Identity Thesis Can and Cannot Mean: Why "God is Freedom" Cannot Be Substituted into the Formula, and What It Means Instead
oa:W7213503803.abstract: Abstract The Philosophy of Virtues makes freedom the substrate of every virtue and holds, as its theological thesis, that God is Freedom. Every formal paper in the programme declares that thesis unused. This article is the exception: it engages the layer in order to constrain it, and the constraint turns out to be structural rather than devotional. The substitution fails, and it fails for a reason internal to the apparatus. The formula V = sgn(F) × D takes three values on its sign — present and self-directed, absent, actively replaced — and the deprivation operator requires a power capable of removing the substrate and receiving the discipline that constituted the act. Substitute the divine name for F and the operator requires a power that can remove God, which is greater than God. The formula demands that its substrate be removable. God is not removable. So the failure is not impiety; it is that a substitutional reading makes every theorem in the corpus vacuous, since inversion, occupation, the three counterfeits and the vacancy results are all built on the possibility of the substrate being taken. The grammar of the predication was never substitutional in the first place, and the tradition supplies the control case. Deus caritas est has been confessed for two millennia, and nobody obtains theology by substituting the divine name into “love is patient and kind.” The identity in such statements is of nature, not of term. One reading survives, and it explains what the formula had assumed. On the participation reading, what God is, is aseity — self-origination with no antecedent, ipsum esse subsistens, the mode of being in which essence and existence are not distinct. oa:W7213586602.title: THE NATURE OF TIME: Trialogue of Science Philosophy and Religion Vision of Time
oa:W7213586602.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7213586602.abstract: The phenomenon of time remains one of the most foundational, recalcitrant, and under-determined categories of human inquiry. While the natural sciences successfully formalize and measure the operational properties of time, they lack a universally accepted ontological definition of what time is at the bedrock of Being. Across philosophy and the theological traditions, time is conceptualized through an extraordinarily disparate spectrum of categories and doctrines. This doctoral dissertation undertakes a disciplined investigation of that ontological lacuna. Its architecture is organized as a systematic trialogue among Science, Philosophy, and Religion. The core methodological principle is rigorous epistemic demarcation: the continuous distinction between established empirical or textual facts and metaphysical or theological postulates adopted on non-empirical rational grounds. oa:W7213859639.title: PAA: The Principle Against Arbitrariness and the Proof of a Threefold God
oa:W7213859639.abstract: This paper asks whether a rigorous demand against arbitrariness can be pushed far enough to yield a substantive conclusion about the structure of reality itself. Beginning from unrestricted exclusion, it develops a cumulative, branch-indexed argument through constitutional closure, fixed-type identity, semantic presence, contingency, sourcehood, and noetic operation. Rather than treating these as interchangeable notions, the paper separates each transition and requires an explicit bridge before moving to a stronger claim. On the paper’s full branch, the argument concludes that there exists exactly one de re necessary, non-derivatively constitutional, minimally noetic source-sovereign with an essential, type-restricted capacity for noetically operated source determination. This conclusion is termed ontological minimal theism. The paper then argues that the bearer’s terminal sovereignty structure has exactly three irreducible orientations: constitutional authority, reflexive noesis, and volitional source-capacity. The broader aim is to show that a strikingly theistic metaphysical profile can emerge from a disciplined analysis of non-arbitrary modal authority rather than from traditional divine-attribute arguments.

oa:W7214001856.title: From Tripartite Freedom to Fair Opportunity: T. H. Green and David O. Brink
oa:W7214001856.abstract: This article examines the structural relationship between T. H. Green’s tripartite conception of freedom and David O. Brink’s fair opportunity account of moral responsibility, arguing that the traces of Green’s model can be discerned in the conceptual architecture of Brink’s account. Green’s conception emerges from a critical engagement with Kant’s account of freedom and responds to Sidgwick’s objection that Kant cannot adequately explain how wrongdoing can be both free and responsible. By identifying moral freedom with the capacity for reasons-responsiveness rather than with its proper exercise, Green defends the spirit of Kantian freedom while addressing its principal weakness. Green distinguishes three dimensions of freedom: juridical freedom as the absence of external coercion; moral freedom as the capacity for reasons-responsiveness that grounds responsibility; and real or perfect freedom as the virtuous actualization of that capacity in pursuit of self-realization and the common good. These three dimensions are not rivals but complementary conditions for the full realization of moral personality. Green’s account of perfect freedom, with its emphasis on self-realization and the common good, also carries a distinctly religious dimension, addressing questions about human nature, divine justice, and moral accountability that situate his tripartite model within the broader concerns of the philosophy of religion. While Berlin’s critique reads Green’s positive freedom as dangerously close to authoritarian justification, and while Weinstein, Simhony, and Dimova-Cookson offer divergent reconstructions of Green’s account, this article takes as its starting point Brink’s reconstruction of Green’s framework within the Kantian tradition. The article shows how Brink’s two centr

oa:W7214021118.title: GeoBalance: Geometry-Aware Monitoring and Reconstruction with Asymmetric Optimization for Balanced Multimodal Learning
oa:W7214021118.abstract: Multimodal classifiers can converge to modality-dominant solutions in which one modality dominates the joint prediction, suppressing the learning of others. Existing balancing methods mainly adjust losses, gradients, or modality contributions, largely treating modality imbalance as an optimization problem while implicitly treating the weak modality as under-optimized but representationally intact. In this work, we find that this assumption does not always hold, as persistent modality dominance can induce a representation-level collapse of the weak modality, which we term \emph{manifold modality collapse} (MMC). MMC manifests as a coupled geometric degradation in which weak-modality representations collapse onto fewer directions within each class and become less separable across classes. Motivated by this observation, we propose \emph{GeoBalance}, a geometry-aware framework that monitors these two geometric properties and reconstructs the weak modality representation only when it exhibits signs of MMC. Once triggered, GeoBalance uses a fixed Simplex-ETF class scaffold and spectral regularization to restore class separation while preventing collapse onto a few feature directions. To preserve reconstruction during joint training, asymmetric gradient projection removes the joint-gradient component conflicting with reconstruction, leaving non-conflicting optimization unchanged. Extensive experiments across six multimodal benchmarks demonstrate great improvements over competitive balancing methods, validating its effectiveness.

oa:W7214028178.title: Fractal Soul: Mapping Sanjuanist Mystical Purifications Through Analogical Structural Isomorphism with Isomorphic Physics
oa:W7214028178.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214028178.abstract: This methodological working paper introduces a rigorous framework of Analogical Structural Isomorphism to map the precise, highly ordered interior geography of the soul’s passive purification as articulated by St. John of the Cross. Grounded in the doctrinal foundations of Thomistic hylomorphism (ST\ I,\ Q.76,\ A.1) and Divine Simplicity (ST\ I,\ Q.3), this study transcends mere poetic metaphor. It positions the laws of the physical universe as lower-resolution pedagogical scaffoldings—the "fingerprints of the Logos"—that mirror the higher-resolution spiritual laws governing the interior life. AI / ASSISTIVE TECHNOLOGY DECLARATIONIn accordance with emerging academic transparency standards and ecclesiastical guidelines for published scholarship, the author discloses the use of generative artificial intelligence (LLM) tools during the preparation of this working paper. AI technology was utilized strictly in an assistive capacity for structural drafting, cross-referencing of canonical texts, comparative stylistic refinement, and formatting optimization. All theological synthesis, canonical interpretations, doctrinal evaluations, and final text selections remain entirely the original work and responsibility of the author.

oa:W7214032233.title: Divine Agency, Will and Freedom in Avicenna
oa:W7214032233.abstract: One of the main criticisms directed at Avicenna’s conception of God in the history of Islamic thought is the claim that he conceived of God as an essentially necessitating cause (mūjib bi-l-dhāt) and thereby eliminated divine will and freedom. This criticism, systematized especially by al-Ghazālī in Tahāfut al-Falāsifa, later became a widespread assumption in kalām and philosophical literature, according to which the Peripatetic philosophers viewed God as a necessary, will-less, and natural cause. This article argues that this assumption should be reconsidered within Avicenna’s own metaphysical system. Its central claim is that Avicenna does not understand divine will as an independent faculty of choice added to God’s essence, but grounds it as an actual perfection to be interpreted together with knowledge, providence, approval, generosity, and wisdom. Based on textual and conceptual analysis, the study first shows the conceptual limits of the binary opposition between the freely choosing agent and the essentially necessitating cause, and then examines the divine attributes within the doctrine of the Necessary Existent. It further argues that emanation should not be read as a natural or mechanical compulsion, but as the necessary perfection of divine knowledge and wisdom. The tension between the kalām theory of choice and the Peripatetic doctrine of necessity is therefore interpreted not as a simple opposition, but as the result of different ontological assumptions about the nature and operation of will. Although al-Ghazālī’s criticisms are strong in terms of their kalām premises, they do not fully capture Avicenna’s specific understanding of will, knowledge, and necessity. In conclusion, Avicenna’s conception of God can be reduced neither to a temporal choosing agent n

oa:W7214508838.title: Unassembled or Partless? The Meaning of Divine Simplicity in the Christian Tradition
oa:W7214508838.abstract: Contemporary accounts frequently describe divine simplicity as a multivalent doctrine encompassing substantially different metaphysical positions. This study investigates whether the Christian tradition nevertheless preserves a stable minimum meaning of simplicity. It distinguishes between two claims: the anti-assembly thesis, according to which God was never produced by combining prior elements, and the stronger partlessness thesis, according to which God possesses no intrinsic constituents at all. Through a survey of representative Christian theologians from the second through the fourteenth centuries, including both orthodox and heterodox participants in major theological controversies and across distinct traditions (such as seen in Duns Scotus and Gregory Palamas), the study examines how simplicity functioned in discussions of divine attributes, Trinitarian distinctions, generation, Christology, formal distinctions, and the divine energies. The sources consistently treat simplicity as excluding both assembly and intrinsic parthood. Their disagreements concern which distinctions constitute parts and how real distinctions can be affirmed without introducing composition into God. Divine simplicity is therefore not multivalent at the level of its minimum metaphysical commitment. Across otherwise divergent accounts, it remains governed by a stable prohibition: God is not constituted by parts. This finding clarifies both the historical meaning of simplicity and the requirements facing contemporary theologians who claim continuity with the Christian tradition.

oa:W7214530047.title: An Information-Processing Framework for Substrates of Consciousness: A Naturalistic Approach to Humans, Artificial Intelligence, and the Question of God
oa:W7214530047.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214530047.abstract: This paper presents an information-processing framework for examining consciousness across biological and artificial substrates. It treats humans and artificial intelligence as information-processing systems implemented on different physical substrates and evaluates claims using methodological naturalism, testability, consistency with established knowledge, and parsimony. The paper examines the epistemic status of several questions at the intersection of philosophy of mind, consciousness science, artificial intelligence, and philosophy of religion. It reviews arguments concerning an interventionist God, including the problem of evil, divine hiddenness, religious diversity, cognitive explanations of religious belief, causal closure, and major theistic responses. It then reviews evidence concerning the dependence of human mental states on brain activity, major scientific theories of consciousness, and current approaches to assessing possible machine consciousness. A further section examines the hypothesis of consciousness transfer between biological and artificial substrates, including questions concerning functionalism, substrate independence, personal identity, whole-brain emulation, and gradual replacement. The paper's main methodological contribution is an epistemic grading framework that distinguishes empirical, theoretical, and philosophical claims according to their evidential support, testability, consistency, and parsimony. The framework emphasizes the distinction between what is empirically established, what is theoretically plausible, and what remains speculative or philosophically contested. This work is a conceptual analysis and literature review rather than an experimental study. It is presented as an open-access research paper and is not represented as a pe

oa:W7214673657.title: Does God have qualia? Some arguments in favour of the existence of divine qualia
oa:W7214673657.abstract: Abstract Does God have qualia, does He know the ‘what it is like’ character of experiences? The questions run deep into the metaphysics of God as they concern concepts that most traditional theists accept with regard to God: that He is personal, loving, omniscient, omnipotent, and created the world ex nihilo . Building upon these concepts, I present four arguments in favour of the existence of divine qualia. Positing divine qualia may seem incompatible with divine simplicity, a tenet of classical theism, and the problem of emotions unworthy of God also may arise. I argue that the difficulties regarding simplicity do not stem from the existence of divine qualia per se but are related to difficulties already established in relation to simplicity. As for emotions unworthy of God, I try to show how a careful distinction between personal perspectives can offer a solution.

oa:W7214677434.title: Presentazione. Rifrazioni dal pensiero di Teodorico Moretti-Costanzi
oa:W7214677434.venue: Nuovo Giornale di Filosofia della Religione (NGFR)
oa:W7214677434.abstract: A trent’anni dalla morte di Teodorico Moretti-Costanzi, il contributo intende richiamare alcuni nuclei fondamentali del suo pensiero e introdurre i saggi raccolti nel fascicolo. Dall’ontologismo critico di Pantaleo Carabellese fino alla formulazione del Cristianesimo-Filosofia, il percorso morettiano si sviluppa come ricerca speculativa del fondamento e come esperienza di verità. I contributi approfondiscono, da prospettive differenti, il rapporto con Carabellese, i temi dell’ascesi, della persona, della mondanità, della verità e le connessioni con l’estetica, l’etica, la filosofia della religione e la teologia. Thirty years after the death of Teodorico Moretti-Costanzi, this contribution recalls some of the fundamental themes of his thought and introduces the essays collected in this issue. From Pantaleo Carabellese’s critical ontologism to the formulation of Christianity-Philosophy, Moretti-Costanzi’s philosophical path develops as a speculative inquiry into foundation and as an experience of truth. The contributions examine, from different perspectives, his relationship with Carabellese, as well as the themes of ascesis, personhood, worldliness, truth, and the connections with aesthetics, ethics, philosophy of religion, and theology.

oa:W7214910569.title: Mercy and Justice in the Context of John 8:1-11: A Philosophy of Religion Perspective
oa:W7214910569.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7214910569.abstract: This paper offers a philosophical evaluation of the relationship between justice and mercy in the narrative of the adulterous woman in John 8:1-11, addressing the central question of whether mercy constitutes a violation or fulfillment of justice. The study begins by situating the narrative within its legal and moral framework, highlighting the apparent retributive demands of Mosaic Law alongside the procedural and ethical deficiencies in its application. Through a rigorous conceptual analysis, the paper engages classical and contemporary philosophical accounts of justice from Aristotelian equity and Kantian retributivism to Rawlsian fairness and Wolterstorff’s rights-based approach while also examining the moral logic of mercy as articulated in both classical theology and modern ethical theory. The analysis argues that the tension between justice and mercy arises primarily from a reductive understanding of justice as strict retribution. By contrast, a broader philosophical framework incorporating equity, dignity, and restorative aims reveals that mercy need not negate justice but can function as its highest expression. Drawing on restorative justice theory and contemporary critiques of punitive models, the paper interprets Jesus’ response as a form of moral intervention that exposes the limitations of legal formalism and reorients justice toward moral transformation. The refusal to condemn the accused, coupled with the call to ethical renewal, reflects a conception of justice that integrates accountability with the possibility of restoration. Within the framework of philosophy of religion, the paper further argues that this narrative provides a coherent account of divine moral action in which justice and mercy are not contradictory but mutually implicative. oa:W7214934757.title: Kant’s Metaphysical Framework: A Critical Study in the Context of the Islamic Conception of Knowledge and Ethics
oa:W7214934757.abstract: This study presents a critical analysis of Immanuel Kant’s metaphysical framework, with particular reference to his theory of knowledge, conception of reason, philosophy of religion, and moral philosophy. It examines the relationship between Kant’s epistemology and his understanding of religion, particularly his distinction between theoretical and practical reason and his restriction of the scope of human reason in metaphysical matters. The study argues that Kant’s separation of faith and reason is closely connected with the intellectual context of rationalist metaphysics and Christian theology. In contrast, the Islamic intellectual tradition approaches knowledge through an integrated relationship among reason, revelation, and human nature (fiṭrah). The study further examines Kant’s moral philosophy, particularly his conception of pure practical reason, the categorical imperative, duty, freedom, and moral responsibility. It argues that morality cannot be adequately grounded in abstract rational principles alone, since moral consciousness, the distinction between good and evil, and the capacity for moral responsibility are rooted in the human self (nafs) and its innate disposition. Drawing upon Qur’anic teachings and Islamic intellectual thought, the study proposes that revelation does not negate innate human knowledge but completes and reinforces the moral and intellectual awareness embedded in human nature. The study concludes that the Islamic conception of knowledge and ethics provides an integrated framework in which reason, revelation, fiṭrah, and the human self operate in a mutually complementary relationship, offering an alternative perspective to Kant’s restricted conception of reason, morality, and metaphysical knowledge.

oa:W7215108450.title: Beyond Performative Morality Based on A Thematic Interpretation of The Satya-Māyā Dialectic in The Ethics of Power of Śakuni and Kṛṣṇa in The Mahābhārata
oa:W7215108450.abstract: The phenomenon of performative morality and religiosity in the contemporary public sphere (moral and religious expressions intended for public consumption, rather than the manifestation of inner dispositions) highlights the need for a conceptual framework that distinguishes between ethical appearance and substance. This research develops a thematic-hermeneutic reading of the satya-māyā dialectic in the Mahābhārata, examining how Śakuni and Kṛṣṇa represent two opposing ethical orientations within the relationship between truth and power. This study of the philosophy of religion employs a hermeneutic-phenomenological approach to the dice-playing episode in the Sabhā Parva and selected ślokas from the Bhagavad Gītā, combined with a comparative analysis drawing on political realism. The results indicate that Śakuni represents the instrumentalisation of truth and morality as tools of power, whilst Kṛṣṇa articulates an ethic that subordinates power to satya and dharma through niṣkāma karma. Māyā is understood as an epistemological condition that enables the disjunction between appearance and essence, whilst sattva and lokasaṅgraha form the textual basis for leadership with integrity. Performative morality and religiosity are formulated as new analytical categories that bridge performativity theory with the conceptual structure of the Bhagavad Gītā, characterised by the gap between appearance and essence, the instrumentalisation of symbols, and visibility, accompanied by critical scrutiny of Kṛṣṇa’s controversial actions, without theological justification. The research concludes that the Mahābhārata offers a model of the ethics of power that positions truth as the foundation (rather than a tool) of leadership legitimacy; a thesis that holds internally within the text’s cosmolo

oa:W7215976613.title: Nothing in God
oa:W7215976613.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
oa:W7215976613.abstract: Classical monotheism describes God as infinite, all-having, and necessarily existent. This paper asks whether these three descriptions can be held together when “all-having” is read strictly, so that it covers not only everything that is but also non-being. I defend a conditional thesis: if divine infinity requires strict inclusion of non-being itself (and not merely of a representation of it), then strict all-inclusiveness, necessary existence, and classical logic cannot all be true of God. The thesis yields a dilemma for theism: either divine all-inclusiveness must be restricted (for instance, to being and to perfections), or God must be placed beyond the constraints of logic. I offer three routes toward the key premise (a completeness argument, a comparison between two conceptions of God, and an argument from specific privations), examine the main objections, and relate the argument to Tillich’s treatment of non-being in God, Cantor’s Absolute Infinite, dialetheic theology, and Aquinas’s objection from contraries. I do not claim to refute theism. The result is a constraint on how the divine attributes may be defined together. Keywords: divine infinity; non-being; necessary existence; omni-inclusiveness; dialetheism; philosophy of religion

oa:W7216211021.title: The Existence of God: A New Way
oa:W7216211021.abstract: Abstract This article addresses the ‘discrepancy issue’ in contemporary analytic philosophy of religion, whereby Richard Swinburne’s probabilistic approach and Graham Oppy’s worldview analysis reach opposing conclusions from substantially the same evidence. In response, it sketches a new abductive argument for God’s existence by developing Peter Lipton’s notion of Inference to the Best Explanation into the method of ‘Virtue-IBE’, which compares rival theories by scoring their theoretical virtues. Virtue-IBE is offered as an improvement upon existing approaches and is applied to Bare Theism, as developed by Swinburne, Worldview Naturalism, as defended by Oppy, and Trope-Theoretic Theism, as proposed in this work (and earlier work), across six broad features of the physical world. On this assessment, Trope-Theoretic Theism, which identifies God as a maximal power trope, emerges as the loveliest, and therefore the best, of the three theories considered. The resulting conjunction of method and theory ultimately provides the basis for a new abductive case for God’s existence.

oa:W7216822697.title: مبانی فلسفی ذات وصفات از نگاه ملاصدرا
oa:W7216822697.abstract: Regarding the divine essence and essential attributes of God, two major perspectives have been proposed. Islamic philosophers prior to Mulla Sadra and Imami theologians maintained the doctrine of the identity of the divine attributes with the divine essence, whereas certain non-Imami theological schools, such as the Ash'arites and the Karramites, upheld the doctrine of the addition of attributes to the essence. By critically examining the views of non-Imami theologians, Sadr al-Din al-Shirazi affirmed the position of earlier Islamic philosophers and Imami theologians, who had rejected multiplicity within the Necessary Being primarily on the basis of the principle of the simplicity of the divine essence. He systematically formulated the theory of the identity of attributes and essence in external reality. Mulla Sadra explained this identity by comparing the relationship between the divine attributes and the divine essence to the relationship between secondary philosophical intelligibles and existence, and by employing the concept of restrictive qualification (ḥaythiyyah taqyīdiyyah). In demonstrating his position, he not only clarified the theoretical difficulties inherent in the doctrine of the addition of attributes to the essence and reformulated them through a disjunctive syllogistic argument, but also advanced additional proofs. Drawing upon his distinctive philosophical principles, particularly the doctrines of the primacy of existence (aṣālat al-wujūd) and the gradation of existence (tashkīk al-wujūd), he succeeded in establishing the identity of the divine attributes and essence. In connection with the discussion of essential attributes, relational and negative attributes are also examined; according to Mulla Sadra’s analysis, these attributes are likewise identi

oa:W7216893590.title: The Cognitivist Paradigm and Its Application in Islamic Religious Education (PAI) Instruction on the Divine Name Al-Khaliq at SDQ Utrujah Pamekasan
oa:W7216893590.abstract: This study aims to describe the implementation of Jean Piaget's cognitivism paradigm in Islamic Education (PAI), specifically regarding the material of Asmaul Husna Al-Khaliq at SD Qur’an Utrujah Pamekasan. The research method used is descriptive phenomenology, involving 25 second-grade elementary students in the concrete operational stage of development as subjects. Data were collected through participatory observation of experimental activities, environmental observations, and bean planting practices, supported by literature analysis. The findings conclude that integrating cognitivism theory using concrete media and interactive methods successfully transforms abstract theological concepts into tangible and rational understanding for students. Students demonstrated the ability to explain the meaning of Al-Khaliq through real-world examples and showed increased emotional engagement and spiritual responsibility for environmental conservation. This approach proved effective in overcoming cognitive barriers faced by young children in understanding divine attributes.

oa:W7217290109.title: تأویل عرفانی و تربیت اخلاقی از منظر امام خمینی (ره): از کشف باطن قرآن تا سلوک عملی
oa:W7217290109.abstract: Mystical hermeneutics within the tradition of Islamic thought is a process through which the spiritual wayfarer advances from the outward form of words to their inner truth, whereby knowledge is elevated to the level of direct witnessing (shuhūd) and moral embodiment (takhalluq). In the thought of Imam Khomeini (1981/2002), this process is neither a mere exegetical technique nor simply an epistemological reflection; rather, it constitutes a socio-ethical structure grounded in existential wayfaring, in which the understanding of the Qur’an is intrinsically interwoven with self-purification and inner moral education. The objective of the present study is to explicate the role of mystical hermeneutics within Imam Khomeini’s intellectual framework and to examine its impact on the formation of moral education and the existential transformation of the monotheistic human being. This qualitative study, through a systematic reexamination of Imam Khomeini’s epistemological and spiritual foundations, demonstrates that the hermeneutical movement in his thought begins with purification of the heart, spiritual vigilance (murāqabah), conscious presence (ḥuḍūr al-qalb), inner struggle (mujāhadah al-nafs), and unwavering commitment to the Sacred Law (Sharīʿah). This path ultimately culminates in the reception of the light of truth and the manifestation of divine attributes within the human being. The findings indicate that within Imam Khomeini’s educational system, acts of worship play a strategic role in transforming knowledge into identity: prayer functions as a discipline of servitude and presence; remembrance (dhikr) serves as an instrument for stabilizing monotheistic awareness; intention constitutes the axis of volitional formation; and ritual ablution (wuḍūʾ) represents the preli

oa:W7217690402.title: ON THE ISSUES OF THE STUDY OF DIVINE NAMES IN ISLAM, CHRISTIANITY AND JUDAISM
oa:W7217690402.abstract: This article conducts a comparative analysis from a linguistic perspective of the role and significance of divine names in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. The sacred texts are examined for the semantic, linguistic, anthropological, and philosophical features of names, as well as their role in shaping religious identity and theological views. Based on the theories of philosophers such as Frege, Russell, Wittgenstein, and Kripke, the relationships between the meaning and reference of names are analyzed. In Judaism, names are considered as signs expressing essence; in Christianity, they are understood in a metaphorical and transcendental sense; and in Islam, they are explored through the 99 names of Allah as a means of revealing divine attributes. The article demonstrates methodological problems through linguistic analysis of comparative issues in religious studies and highlights the potential for creating a common language for interreligious dialogue.

oa:W7217702849.title: Divine Simplicity: The Aspectival Account
oa:W7217702849.venue: European Journal for Philosophy of Religion
oa:W7217702849.abstract: This article aims to provide a consistent explication of the doctrine of Divine Simplicity. To achieve this end, a re-construal of the doctrine is made within an “aspectival trope-theoretic” metaphysical framework, which will ultimately enable the doctrine to be elucidated in a consistent manner, and the Plantingian objections raised against it will be shown to be unproblematic.

oa:W7219305632.title: Penser la religion à partir de la vie : au-delà des approches théologiques et positivistes, la troisième voie philosophique bergsonienne
oa:W7219305632.abstract: In this article, we aim to highlight the uniqueness and originality of Bergson's approach to religion, as presented and developed in The Two Sources of Morality and Religion (1932). We will examine the critical dialogues that took place between Bergson and various interlocutors on this issue: first, the dialogue between Bergson and proponents of the theological approach, and then his exchanges with advocates of a more positivist approach to religion, such as those found in sociology or clinical psychology. We will then show that Bergson’s philosophy of religion, by grounding itself in the concept of life to capture the significance of religious experiences in human existence, lays the foundations for what could be called a religious vitalism, thereby engaging with and converging toward the thought of the American pragmatist philosopher William James.

oa:W7219363887.title: Погляд Алвіна Плантінги на природню теологію як підставу протистояння віри і розуму в проблемі доказу існування бога
oa:W7219363887.venue: Філософія та політологія в контексті сучасної культури
oa:W7219363887.abstract: The article deals with analytical and theological concept of Alvin Plantinga in the context of American and European philosophical thought.The key idea of the article is to identify the relations between faith and reason, as well as the specifis of their interaction in the analytical and theological concept A. Plantinga.The proposed methodology: the method of comparative analysis; the method of historical and philosophical analysis; the hermeneutical method; the phenomenological method.A. Plantinga emphasizes that the evidentialist objection and the Thomistic conception of faith and knowledge can be traced back to a common root in classical foundationalism – a pervasive and widely accepted picture or total way of looking at faith, knowledge, belief, rationality. According to the evidentialist objection belief in God is unreasonable and irrational because there is insuffiient evidence for it. The evidentialists have endorsed the idea that the strength of one’s belief ought always to be proportional to the strength of the evidence for that belief. oa:W7219394791.title: METAFİZİKSEL SONSUZLUK VE TANRI: İLAHİ SONSUZLUĞUN MAHİYETİNE DAİR BİR İNCELEME
oa:W7219394791.venue: Euroasia Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities
oa:W7219394791.abstract: The concept of infinity has been employed in a wide variety of meanings throughout the history of philosophy. Nevertheless, discussions concerning divine infinity have often been influenced by mathematical or quantitative conceptions of infinity, and divine infinity has generally been understood in terms of the infinity or unlimitedness of the divine attributes. This article aims to examine divine infinity as directly expressive of God's mode of being, that is, on the basis of a conception of metaphysical infinity. To this end, the fundamental differences between mathematical infinity and metaphysical infinity will first be identified, after which the implications of applying metaphysical infinity to God will be explored. Within this framework, it will be argued that divine infinity cannot be reduced to the notion of the unlimitedness of divine attributes; rather, it should be understood as a fundamental principle expressing God's mode of being.

oa:W7219403724.abstract: The article deals with philosophical and theological concept of Alvin Plantinga in the context of European metaphysics. The key idea of the article is the problem of proof for the existence of God in the analytical concept of A.Plantinga.The proposed methodology: the method of historical and philosophical analysis; the phenomenological method; the hermeneutical method; the method of comparative analysis.The author researches philosophical basis of the problem of proof for the existence of God in the thought of the most prominent philosopher of the 13th century, St. Thomas Aquinas and Alvin Plantinga’s analytic philosophy.The author of the article points out that Plantinga’s ontology contains two levels: the level of possible worlds, and the level of objects.The article emphasizes that A.Plantinga develops the concept of basic religious beliefs. It is described in short that God is a personal being who has created the world, who has no beginning, and who is perfect in wisdom, justice, knowledge, and power. It is introduced the distinction between belief in God and belief in the existence of God. The article stresses the difference between the simplicity of God in the opinion of Aquinas and the simplicity of God in the Plantinga’s opinion. oa:W747113379.title: Being, becoming, and God : toward a relational theology : a study in the doctrine of God, with special reference to the thought of John Macquarrie and Charles Hartshorne
oa:W747113379.venue: St Andrews Research Repository (St Andrews Research Repository)
oa:W747113379.abstract:
This study in the doctrine of God, with special reference to the thought of John Macquarrie and Charles Hartshorne, addresses the issue of the relational problematic and suggests a potential resolution. 
The 'Relational Problematic' focusses on the notion of aseity and the doctrine of the Trinity. It concerns the ontological conundrum posed by, on the one hand, the insistence that the external relations God has are of no ontological consequence to him, together with, on the other hand, the witness of the Christian tradition that suggests such relations are not, in fact, inconsequential for the being of God. The task of constructing a resolution begins with the ontology of the early Heidegger which is implicitly relational. Thus 'relational ontology' furnishes a hermeneutical key whereby a 'Relational Theology' may be developed. 
This development involves, first, the analysis of John Macquarrie's existential- ontological theism, which concludes that to speak of God in the language of 'Being' is to speak of the relational being of God. Second, and alongside this, is placed the analysis and discussion of the neoclassical theism of Charles Hartshorne: the pluriform language of Becoming by which God is conceived in process thought has at its base the perception of the essential relatedness of God. But both Macquarrie and Hartshorne have as a common problem the question of the "entitative status" of God. The solution is suggested by way of conceiving God as "Relational Entity" . The 'Being' and the 'Becoming' of God are manifest in ad extra relatedness: such relationality forms the fundamental ontological motif in the conception of God.

oa:W750690483.title: The Freedom of God For Us : Karl Barth's Doctrine of Divine Aseity
oa:W750690483.abstract: This volume provides an analysis of divine aseity in Karl Barth’s thought and appreciates the vital role that this doctrine can play in contemporary theology. Brian D. Asbill begins by setting the general theological context, first through a broad sketch of the development of Barth’s understanding of the relationship between the life of God pro nobis (pronobeity) anda se (aseity), and secondly through the examination of the basic theological convictions that guide his approach to the divine being in Church Dogmatics II/1. The second section, ‘The Love and Freedom of God’, turns to the dialectical pairings which guide Barth’s accounts of the divine reality in his earliest dogmatic cycle (The Göttingen Dogmatics §§16–7) as well as in his most mature treatment (Church Dogmatics §§28–31). oa:W759743966.title: Suárez’s Doctrine of Concepts: How Divine and Human Intellection are Intertwined
oa:W759743966.abstract: For any scholastic philosopher, divine and human intellection are deeply intertwined. After all, God knows things before man does, and even before they exist. This makes God's knowledge the model for human knowledge. The main difficulty with respect to God's knowledge is how to reconcile His independence and simplicity with His knowledge of a plurality of things. The way in which a scholastic philosopher handles this difficulty determines how divine intellection works, and, consequently, how human intellection works. Francisco Suarez examines the traditional positions on this matter very closely, in order to develop his own solution. From the many positions that are important for him, the first half of this chapter presents those of Thomas Aquinas, John Duns Scotus, and William of Ockham, corresponding to the Thomist, Scotist, and Nominalist schools. The second half is dedicated to Suarez 's own solution. Keywords: divine; Francisco Suarez; human intellection; John Duns Scotus; Thomas Aquinas; William of Ockham

oa:W763132208.title: John Howe (1630–1705) on Divine Simplicity: A Debate over Spinozism
oa:W763132208.abstract: Seventeenth-century Reformed theology faced a radical challenge from Cartesian notions of substance and simplicity. This chapter demonstrates that John Howe's attack on Spinoza's teaching of divine simplicity is indicative of Reformed efforts to restate the compatibility of divine simplicity with divine attributes, and, contrary to some modern readings, establishes the point that 'simplicity' as understood in the era of Protestant orthodoxy did not entail an absence of distinctions in the Godhead. It first identifies an emergence of Spinozism and its implication for the notion of simplicity in the late seventeenth century. The chapter then shows how Howe responded to Spinoza's monistic argument in order to vindicate the distinctions of divine attributes. These examinations clarify that a different appropriation of the notion of simplicity came into being in the late seventeenth century and Howe responded to the new interpretation by restating a traditional Reformed understanding of divine simplicity. Keywords: divine simplicity; John Howe; protestant orthodoxy; seventeenth-century reformed theology; Spinoza's teaching

oa:W777931004.title: The Challenge of God
oa:W777931004.abstract: “Classical theism,” refers to St. Thomas Aquinas’ Summa Theologica, which is also known as the Doctrine of God. Over time there have been many people who have affirmed Aquinas’ teachings about God, while others have strongly disagreed and worked to disprove him. Aquinas’ critics often try to debunk one if not all of the seven attributes he gives to God: simplicity, impassability, immutability, perfection, infinite, eternal, and his oneness. The final six attributes all stem from God’s simplicity, and if any of them can be disproven then simplicity is also disproven thus rendering all of Aquinas’ work in the De Deo Uno invalid. Unfortunately these critics misunderstand the purpose of the De Deo Uno; it is meant to be a guide for what language we use about God, not a definitive definition for Him. In addition to misunderstanding the mission of the De Deo Uno these critics also overlook the very topic Aquinas stressed the most: we can never truly know God’s essence because God is beyond our abilities to comprehend.

oa:W868145005.title: Aquinas on Essence, Existence, and Divine Simplicity - Strange but Consistent
oa:W868145005.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to find an interpretation on which several of Aquinas’ metaphysical commitments are consistent. One commitment is that God is his essence; another is that God is his existence (i.e. his being); and the last is that God is simple. Aquinas concludes from the first two that, in God, essence and existence are identical. The first objection in Summa Theologiae 3.4 in effect leads this conclusion in a pantheistic direction. For, it challenges Aquinas to find a difference between God’s existence and the existence of everything else. If Aquinas cannot find such a difference then, if God’s existence and essence are the same and if God’s existence is the same as the existence of everything else, then it follows that God’s essence is the same as the existence of everything else, which means that everything has God’s essence. This leads to a type of pantheism that Aquinas surely would not embrace.  In this paper I argue that there is exactly one possible way in which God’s existence is different from the existence of everything else: God’s existence is pure actuality whereas the existence of everything else is actuality but not pure actuality. This argument requires me to enumerate several of Aquinas’ metaphysical principles, some found in the Summa Theologiae , others in On Being and Essence , which I do in the first half of the paper. In the second half I show why the difference between these two types of existence can only be in terms of actuality.

oa:W975661916.title: Divine simplicity as a problem for orthodoxy
oa:W975661916.abstract: ‘The evolution of orthodoxy’ might easily be understood as a process which belongs wholly to the past: the development of Christian doctrine, on which Henry Chadwick has shed such a graceful and penetrating light, would then be contrasted with a complete and stable construction in which Christianity has come to rest. But to call it complete and stable need not mean that further progress is excluded; at the very least, new challenges are likely to arise, and old truths will need to be re-stated. And most of our generation, and of our juniors, will think this programme far too tame: in their eyes, only an obstinate and secluded mind will persist in defending an orthodoxy that is purely static. I for one would certainly wish to see its evolution as a continuing process, in which established positions need to be clarified and some false steps retracted, in the faith that a better grounded and better articulated consensus of belief may be attained. From such a standpoint one can turn with a rueful admiration to a handbook which has given invaluable service to a succession of beginners in theology, the Enchiridion Patristicum of M. J. Rouet de Journel, completed in 1911 and appearing in its twenty-fourth edition in 1969.

oa:W993112017.title: D'Afrique en Amérique. La migration d'Esu le Décepteur.
oa:W993112017.abstract: Starting from the african mythology of ESHU, the Yorubas' deceitful god who plays a key-part in black Africa as creator of an ever changing order and as introducer of a kind of divination based upon numbers, we may decipher striking conformities with the case of Hermes. The black migration to America retains ESHU' s very substantial reality, as the incarnation of the ASE (vital impetus), that tends to blend with the Christian devil.
